modules.title: Arrival
modules.theme: First day on the ice: get the first services running in containers

missions.title: First Light
missions.story:
RADIO, 06:42. Ingrid Halvorsen on the handset, static in the background.

"Engineer, you made it off the ferry. Good. The old server coughed twice overnight and I no longer trust anything it tells me. Tomasz installed a fresh Docker engine on the new machine, but nobody has run a single thing on it yet."

"Before I move one instrument over, I want proof that it works. Run a throwaway container from `alpine:3.20`, name it `first-light`, and have it print KESTREL POINT ONLINE. Then let it finish by itself. Show me it ended cleanly."
objectives: Run a container named `first-light` from `alpine:3.20` that prints `KESTREL POINT ONLINE`
The container must have finished on its own with exit code 0 (it will show as Exited in `docker ps -a`)
missions.startingState: A freshly installed Docker engine with no containers yet. The shell opens in an empty /workspace.
hints: `docker run` creates a container and starts it, running one command inside. A command that ends quickly leaves a stopped container behind, and `docker ps -a` is the way to see stopped ones.
The shape is `docker run --name <name> <image> <command>`. Use `echo` as the command to print text; a command that succeeds exits with code 0.

```bash
docker run --name first-light alpine:3.20 echo "KESTREL POINT ONLINE"
docker ps -a --filter name=first-light
```

validation.description: Container `first-light` has stopped with exit code 0
The output of `first-light` contains `KESTREL POINT ONLINE`

solution: docker run --name first-light alpine:3.20 echo "KESTREL POINT ONLINE"
missions.debrief: A container lives exactly as long as its main process: `echo` finished, so the container stopped, yet it stays on disk until you remove it. Pro tip: add `--rm` to throwaway runs so they clean up after themselves.

missions.title: Keep the Beacon Lit
missions.story:
NORA // 03:15 // ALERT. STATUS PAGE: DOWN. LAST HOST: OLD-SERVER. UPTIME RECORD: BROKEN.

The monitoring bot has been serving the station's status page from a server that now reboots every few hours. Each time it drops, the crew loses sight of the generators and the greenhouse heaters.

Give the page a new home. Start `nginx:alpine` as a container called `beacon`, and run it in the background. Ingrid wants the terminal back for the next job, and the beacon has to keep burning while you work.
objectives: Run `nginx:alpine` as a container named `beacon`
The container must be running in the background (detached), not holding your terminal
missions.startingState: Docker is installed and no containers exist. The `nginx:alpine` image is already downloaded.
hints: A container started normally is attached to your terminal and stops being useful the moment you press Ctrl+C. Docker can detach a container so it runs in the background.
Combine the detach flag `-d` with `--name` before the image: `docker run -d --name <name> <image>`. Check the result with `docker ps`.

```bash
docker run -d --name beacon nginx:alpine
docker ps
```

validation.description: The web server inside `beacon` answers on its own port 80

missions.debrief: Detached mode (`-d`) starts the container's main process in the background and prints the container ID. Pro tip: `docker logs -f beacon` lets you watch a detached container without attaching to it.

missions.title: The Noticeboard
missions.story:
Taped to the side of the rack, in Kip's round handwriting:

"The noticeboard lived on port 8081 of the old server and now it is just gone?? Everybody's bookmarks point at :8081. Sauna rota, ferry dates, who stole the last of the good coffee. It's the Apache one (`httpd:2.4-alpine`). Please bring it back!! - Kip"

Below it, in Ingrid's neat hand: "Same port as before. The container is called `noticeboard`."
objectives: Run `httpd:2.4-alpine` detached as a container named `noticeboard`
Publish it so that `http://localhost:8081` reaches the web server (container port 80)
missions.startingState: No containers exist. The `httpd:2.4-alpine` image is already downloaded.
hints: A container has its own private network. To reach a service inside it from the outside, you publish one of its ports on the host.
The publish flag is `-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT`. The Apache image listens on port 80 inside the container, and the crew expects 8081 on the outside.

```bash
docker run -d --name noticeboard -p 8081:80 httpd:2.4-alpine
curl http://localhost:8081
```
missions.debrief: `-p 8081:80` maps host port 8081 to container port 80, so the left number is what clients use and the right one is what the app listens on. Pro tip: `docker port noticeboard` prints the active mappings.

missions.title: Calibrate the Sensor
missions.story:
From: Amara Okafor
Subject: sensor-sim needs real settings

The simulator reads its configuration from environment variables instead of a config file, because that is faster to tweak. It wants STATION, UNITS and INTERVAL. Without them it falls back to defaults and reports temperatures in furlongs. (Don't ask.)

Start a container named `sensor-sim` in the background with STATION=kestrel, UNITS=metric and INTERVAL=30. Until my real image is done, use `alpine:3.20` and this stand-in command, which echoes the settings it sees: `sh -c 'echo calibrated $STATION/$UNITS/$INTERVAL; sleep infinity'`
objectives: Run `sensor-sim` detached from `alpine:3.20` with `STATION=kestrel`, `UNITS=metric` and `INTERVAL=30` set
Use the stand-in command `sh -c 'echo calibrated $STATION/$UNITS/$INTERVAL; sleep infinity'` so the log shows `calibrated kestrel/metric/30`
missions.startingState: No containers exist. Nothing is configured yet.
hints: Containers receive configuration through environment variables. You pass each one at `docker run` time, and the program inside sees it exactly as if it had been exported in a shell.
Use one `-e NAME=value` per variable, placed before the image name. Wrap the stand-in command in single quotes so your own shell does not expand `$STATION` first.

```bash
docker run -d --name sensor-sim \
  -e STATION=kestrel -e UNITS=metric -e INTERVAL=30 \
  alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo calibrated $STATION/$UNITS/$INTERVAL; sleep infinity'
docker logs sensor-sim
```
solution: docker run -d --name sensor-sim -e STATION=kestrel -e UNITS=metric -e INTERVAL=30 alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo calibrated $STATION/$UNITS/$INTERVAL; sleep infinity'
missions.debrief: Environment variables let one image behave differently per deployment without rebuilding it. Pro tip: `docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Env}}' sensor-sim` shows exactly what a container was started with.

missions.title: Static on the Radio
missions.story:
LOG EXCERPT, radio-bridge: "sweep 1: carrier lost, static on all bands ... sweep 2: carrier lost, static on all bands ... sweep 3 ..." and about 600 lines more like it.

The radio bridge runs as a container called `radio-static`, and it has logged every crackle for the past hour. Somewhere in that noise it printed, exactly once, the code of the mainland relay. Rafael needs that code before the *Petrel* can sail.

Tomasz scrolled for ten minutes and gave up. The line you want contains the word LOCK. Find it in the container's logs and write only the code itself into `/workspace/frequency.txt`.
objectives: Find the line containing `LOCK` in the logs of the running container `radio-static`
Write just the relay code (nothing else) into `/workspace/frequency.txt`
missions.startingState: A container named `radio-static` is running and has already produced several hundred log lines.
hints: Everything a container writes to its output is captured by Docker. The command family is `docker logs`, and you can pipe it into the usual text tools.
Filter with `grep LOCK`. Careful: the bridge reports its important lines on stderr, and a plain pipe only carries stdout, so redirect with `2>&1` before the pipe.

```bash
docker logs radio-static 2>&1 | grep LOCK
# copy the code= value, then:
echo "THE-CODE" > /workspace/frequency.txt
```

commands: docker run -d --name radio-static alpine:3.20 sh -c 'i=1; while [ $i -le 600 ]; do echo "[radio-bridge] sweep $i: carrier lost, static on all bands"; if [ $i -eq 301 ]; then echo "[radio-bridge] RELAY-LOCK mainland relay acquired, code=KP-4417-ICE" >&2; fi; i=$((i+1)); done; sleep infinity'

validation.description: `/workspace/frequency.txt` does not contain pasted log noise

solution: docker logs radio-static 2>&1 | grep LOCK | sed 's/.*code=//' > /workspace/frequency.txt
missions.debrief: `docker logs` replays a container's stdout and stderr, and the output pipes like any other command. Pro tip: `--tail 20` and `--since 10m` trim a noisy log before you even reach for grep.

missions.title: Inside the Thermostat
missions.story:
Tomasz: The cold-room thermostat reads setpoint 25. It must be 18. Core samples cannot sit above 20.

You: Can I restart the container with new settings?

Tomasz: No. It has been recording since this morning, and its calibration log lives in the container's own temp files. A restart-and-recreate would erase the day's curve. Change the value inside the running container. The file is `/etc/thermostat/thermostat.conf` in the container `thermostat`; `setpoint=25` has to become `setpoint=18`.
objectives: Change `setpoint=25` to `setpoint=18` in `/etc/thermostat/thermostat.conf` inside the container `thermostat`
Keep the same container running: do not remove or recreate it
missions.startingState: A container named `thermostat` is running with `setpoint=25` in its config and a calibration log at `/tmp/calibration.log`.
hints: You can run an extra command inside a container that is already running without touching its main process. That command family is `docker exec`.
The shape is `docker exec <container> <command>`. A one-line `sed -i 's/old/new/' file` edits a file without opening an editor; `cat` lets you verify the result.

```bash
docker exec thermostat cat /etc/thermostat/thermostat.conf
docker exec thermostat sed -i 's/setpoint=25/setpoint=18/' /etc/thermostat/thermostat.conf
docker exec thermostat cat /etc/thermostat/thermostat.conf
```

commands: docker run -d --name thermostat alpine:3.20 sh -c 'mkdir -p /etc/thermostat; echo setpoint=25 > /etc/thermostat/thermostat.conf; echo "day curve: 22 23 25" > /tmp/calibration.log; sleep infinity'

validation.description: The original container survived: `/tmp/calibration.log` still exists

missions.debrief: `docker exec` starts a second process inside the same container, so it can inspect or repair a live service. Pro tip: changes made this way vanish if the container is recreated, so also fix the source of the config afterwards.

missions.title: Generator Rotation
missions.story:
SHIFT HANDOVER SHEET, GENERATOR ROOM, initialled I.H.
[ ] gen-alpha: 400 hours without a break, stand it down
[ ] gen-bravo: rested and ready, bring it online
[ ] gen-charlie: crashed overnight, clear out the wreckage

The three generator services were moved into containers last night. Ingrid went to bed after signing the sheet, so the list is yours. Work through it top to bottom. `docker ps -a` shows every container, running or not, and you will need it to see which one is which.
objectives: Stop `gen-alpha` (it must still exist, just not running)
Start `gen-bravo` so that it is running
Remove `gen-charlie` completely
missions.startingState: `gen-alpha` is running, `gen-bravo` is stopped, and `gen-charlie` has crashed and exited with an error.
hints: Containers move between states: running, stopped, and removed. Each transition has its own command, and a stopped container still shows up in `docker ps -a`.
Three separate verbs do the work: `docker stop`, `docker start` and `docker rm`, each followed by the container name. Removing is not the same thing as stopping.

```bash
docker ps -a
docker stop gen-alpha
docker start gen-bravo
docker rm gen-charlie
docker ps -a
```

commands: docker run -d --name gen-alpha alpine:3.20 sh -c 'trap "exit 0" TERM; while :; do sleep 1; done'
docker run -d --name gen-bravo alpine:3.20 sh -c 'trap "exit 0" TERM; while :; do sleep 1; done'
docker run --name gen-charlie alpine:3.20 sh -c 'exit 3' || true

missions.debrief: Stopping is not deleting: a stopped container keeps its filesystem and logs until `docker rm` takes it away for good. Pro tip: `docker container prune` sweeps every stopped container at once, so run it only when nothing in `docker ps -a` still matters.

missions.title: Weather the Storm
missions.story:
INCIDENT REPORT #031, filed by Ingrid Halvorsen.

What happened: a wind gust cut grid power for four seconds at 02:10. The server rebooted and every container stayed down until someone logged in. We lost three hours of anemometer readings.

What must change: the wind logger, currently running as `wlog-tmp` (Kip's "temporary" name from last week), has to come back by itself after a reboot, unless someone stopped it on purpose. The dashboards also expect the name `wind-logger`. Do not recreate it: its buffer file holds readings that have not been sent yet.
objectives: Make the running container restart automatically with the `unless-stopped` policy
Rename `wlog-tmp` to `wind-logger` (it must keep running, and the old name must be gone)
missions.startingState: A container named `wlog-tmp` is running with no restart policy and holds an unsent-readings buffer at `/tmp/readings.buf`.
hints: Both changes can be made to a container that already exists, so there is no need to remove it. Look for `docker update` for settings and `docker rename` for names.

The restart behaviour is set with `docker update --restart <policy> <container>`. The policy you want keeps the container alive across reboots but respects a manual stop. Rename takes the old name, then the new one.

```bash
docker update --restart unless-stopped wlog-tmp
docker rename wlog-tmp wind-logger
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy.Name}}' wind-logger
```

commands: docker run -d --name wlog-tmp alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo 12.4kn > /tmp/readings.buf; sleep infinity'

validation.description: The old name `wlog-tmp` no longer exists
It is the original container: `/tmp/readings.buf` is still there

missions.debrief: `docker update` changes restart policy and resource limits on a live container, and `docker rename` changes its name without a restart. Pro tip: `unless-stopped` beats `always` for most services because a deliberate `docker stop` survives a daemon restart.

modules.title: Instrument Images
modules.theme: Package every instrument's software into proper images

missions.title: Supplies from the Mainland
missions.story:
PETREL CARGO MANIFEST, voyage 114. Item 22: one "toolbox", contents: software. Delivery: by network, because the ship's hold is full of fuel drums. Signed, Captain Rafael Duarte. Scribbled underneath: "Satellite window opens in ten minutes. Pull it then, not later."

Ingrid's reply is clipped to the page. Tomasz's old scripts were only tested against BusyBox 1.36, not the newer release already on the machine, so pull exactly `busybox:1.36`. Then give it the station's own name, `kestrel/toolbox:1.0`, so the whole crew refers to one tag. Keep the original tag as well.
objectives: Pull the image `busybox:1.36` from the registry
Create a second tag `kestrel/toolbox:1.0` that points at the very same image
missions.startingState: The machine has several images pre-loaded, but `busybox:1.36` is not one of them.
hints: Images are downloaded from a registry, and every image can carry more than one name (tag). Downloading and renaming are two different commands.
Use `docker pull NAME:TAG` to fetch a specific version, and `docker tag SOURCE TARGET` to add a new name to an image that is already local.

```bash
docker pull busybox:1.36
docker tag busybox:1.36 kestrel/toolbox:1.0
docker images
```

params.command: [ "$(docker image inspect -f '{{.Id}}' busybox:1.36)" = "$(docker image inspect -f '{{.Id}}' kestrel/toolbox:1.0)" ] && echo SAME-IMAGE

validation.description: `kestrel/toolbox:1.0` and `busybox:1.36` are the same image (identical ID)

missions.debrief: A tag is just a movable label on an image, and `docker tag` adds a name without copying any data. Pro tip: always pull a specific tag, since `latest` can change underneath you.

missions.title: A Recipe for Greetings
missions.story:
#general, 09:12.

Kip: ok so I wrote a script that prints the morning greeting on the lobby screen and it works on my laptop!!! Amara says that is "not a deployment". what is a Dockerfile??

Amara: Kip's script is `/workspace/greet.sh`. Write a Dockerfile that starts from `alpine:3.20`, copies the script into the image, and makes it the default command. Build it as `kestrel/greeter:1.0`. If a plain `docker run kestrel/greeter:1.0` greets the lobby, Kip has shipped their first image.
objectives: Write `/workspace/Dockerfile` that starts `FROM alpine:3.20`, copies `greet.sh` into the image and runs it by default
Build the image with the tag `kestrel/greeter:1.0`
missions.startingState: `/workspace/greet.sh` exists and is executable. There is no Dockerfile yet.
hints: A Dockerfile is a text file of build instructions. Each instruction adds a step, and `docker build` turns the file plus a folder of files (the build context) into an image.

You need three instructions: `FROM` for the starting image, `COPY` to bring `greet.sh` in from the build context, and `CMD` for what runs by default. Then `docker build -t NAME:TAG .` from the folder that holds the Dockerfile.

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY greet.sh /app/greet.sh
CMD ["/app/greet.sh"]
EOF
docker build -t kestrel/greeter:1.0 .
docker run --rm kestrel/greeter:1.0
```

files.content:
#!/bin/sh
echo "Good morning, Kestrel Point! Sunrise in 41 minutes. Wind 12 knots from the north."

validation.description: Running `kestrel/greeter:1.0` with no arguments prints the greeting

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY greet.sh /app/greet.sh
CMD ["/app/greet.sh"]
EOF
missions.debrief: Your script now ships with its own runtime: `FROM` chose the base, `COPY` brought the file in and `CMD` decided what runs. Pro tip: keep the build context small and the Dockerfile at its root, so a plain `docker build .` always works.

missions.title: Tools for the Field Kit
missions.story:
FIELD KIT PACKING LIST, laminated, signed I. Halvorsen.
[x] Boots, two pairs
[x] Satellite phone
[ ] `curl`, to poll the weather feed
[ ] `jq`, to read what the feed sends back

The last two are software. The field laptops run a container image, and plain `alpine:3.20` ships with neither tool. Build `kestrel/fieldkit:1.0` on top of `alpine:3.20` with both installed. Alpine's package manager is `apk`, and the satellite link is slow, so keep the image under 30 MB.
objectives: Write `/workspace/Dockerfile` based on `alpine:3.20` that installs `curl` and `jq` with `apk`
Build the image as `kestrel/fieldkit:1.0` and keep it under 30 MB
missions.startingState: An empty /workspace. The machine has internet access for downloading Alpine packages.
hints: Installing software while building an image is done with a `RUN` instruction, which executes a command during the build and saves the result in the image.
On Alpine the install command is `apk add`. Add `--no-cache` so the package index is not stored in the image, and list both tools in one `RUN` line.

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache curl jq
EOF
docker build -t kestrel/fieldkit:1.0 .
docker run --rm kestrel/fieldkit:1.0 jq --version
```

validation.description: The image is smaller than 30 MB

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache curl jq
EOF
missions.debrief: `RUN` executes during the build and bakes the result into a new layer, and `--no-cache` keeps apk's index files out of that layer. Pro tip: combine related installs in one `RUN` so they share a single layer.

missions.title: Celsius or Fahrenheit
missions.story:
NORA: UNIT MISMATCH. SENSOR GRID REPORTS CELSIUS. LEGACY DISPLAYS EXPECT FAHRENHEIT. FOURTEEN DISPLAYS SHOWING GARBAGE. CONVERTER SCRIPT FOUND AT /WORKSPACE/CONVERT.SH. NO IMAGE FOUND. NO OWNER FOUND.

Amara's script takes a Celsius value as its first argument and defaults to 0. Package it as `kestrel/converter:1.0` so the image behaves like a command: `docker run kestrel/converter:1.0 100` must print `212.0 F`, and with no argument at all it must convert the default 0 and print `32.0 F`.

The trick is making the arguments replace the default instead of being appended to it.
objectives: Build `kestrel/converter:1.0` from `alpine:3.20` containing `convert.sh`
`docker run kestrel/converter:1.0` prints `32.0 F` (default argument 0)
`docker run kestrel/converter:1.0 100` prints `212.0 F` (argument replaces the default)
missions.startingState: `/workspace/convert.sh` exists and is executable. No Dockerfile has been written.
hints: Two Dockerfile instructions control what runs at start: one fixes the program itself, the other supplies default arguments that anything after the image name replaces.
Put the script in `ENTRYPOINT` using the JSON (exec) form, and the default value in `CMD`, also in JSON form. Whatever you type after the image name replaces `CMD` only.

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY convert.sh /app/convert.sh
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/convert.sh"]
CMD ["0"]
EOF
docker build -t kestrel/converter:1.0 .
docker run --rm kestrel/converter:1.0 100
```

files.content:
#!/bin/sh
awk -v c="${1:-0}" 'BEGIN { printf "%.1f F\n", c * 9 / 5 + 32 }'

validation.description: With no arguments the image prints `32.0 F`
With the argument `100` the image prints `212.0 F`

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY convert.sh /app/convert.sh
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/convert.sh"]
CMD ["0"]
EOF
missions.debrief: `ENTRYPOINT` is the fixed program and `CMD` is its default arguments, which `docker run IMAGE args` replaces. Pro tip: `docker run --entrypoint sh` overrides the entrypoint itself when you need to debug an image.

missions.title: Label the Crates
missions.story:
Taped to crate 0417, in Tomasz's capital letters:

THE INVENTORY SYSTEM READS METADATA FROM THE IMAGE, NOT FROM ANYONE'S MEMORY. EVERY CRATE IMAGE NEEDS A STATION LABEL, ITS OWN CRATE ID, AND A KNOWN WORKING DIRECTORY. THE CRATE ID MUST NOT BE TYPED INTO THE FILE; IT IS PASSED IN AT BUILD TIME, OR WE WILL FORGET TO CHANGE IT.

Build `kestrel/crate:2.0` from `alpine:3.20` with a label `station=kestrel-point`, a label and an environment variable both carrying the crate ID `C-0417` (supplied as a build argument), and the working directory `/crate`.
objectives: Build `kestrel/crate:2.0` from `alpine:3.20` with `docker build --build-arg CRATE_ID=C-0417`
Label `station=kestrel-point` and label `crate-id` equal to the build argument value
Environment variable `CRATE_ID` equal to the same value, and `WORKDIR /crate`
missions.startingState: An empty /workspace. No Dockerfile exists.
hints: Image metadata is set by Dockerfile instructions that describe the image rather than doing work. A build-time variable is declared with one instruction and fed a value from the command line.

Declare `ARG CRATE_ID`, then reuse it as `$CRATE_ID` in `ENV` and `LABEL`. Use `WORKDIR` for the directory, and pass the value with `docker build --build-arg NAME=value`. Give the ARG a default like `UNASSIGNED` so a forgotten flag is obvious.

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
ARG CRATE_ID=UNASSIGNED
LABEL station="kestrel-point" crate-id="$CRATE_ID"
ENV CRATE_ID=$CRATE_ID
WORKDIR /crate
EOF
docker build --build-arg CRATE_ID=C-0417 -t kestrel/crate:2.0 .
```

validation.description: Environment variable `CRATE_ID=C-0417` is set in the image

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
ARG CRATE_ID=UNASSIGNED
LABEL station="kestrel-point" crate-id="$CRATE_ID"
ENV CRATE_ID=$CRATE_ID
WORKDIR /crate
EOF
missions.debrief: `ARG` exists only while building, while `ENV` persists into containers and `LABEL` records metadata that tools can query. Pro tip: read labels back with `docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Labels}}' IMAGE | jq`.

missions.title: Leave the Secrets Ashore
missions.story:
RADIO, 11:58. Rafael Duarte, wind in the microphone.

"Engineer, the mainland lab pulls whatever image you hand me, and they scan it. Last time they found a credentials file inside and sent it straight back. Slow link, no second chances."

The `/workspace` folder holds the outbound report, a `secrets.env` full of credentials, and a 40 MB `raw/` folder of ice-dump data. The provided Dockerfile copies the whole folder with `COPY . /app`. Build `kestrel/outbound:1.0` from it so the report goes out and neither `secrets.env` nor `raw/` does. Do not change the Dockerfile.
objectives: Create `/workspace/.dockerignore` that excludes `secrets.env` and `raw`
Build the existing Dockerfile as `kestrel/outbound:1.0` (the image must be under 20 MB)
The image must contain `report.txt` but neither `secrets.env` nor `raw`
missions.startingState: `/workspace` contains a Dockerfile (`COPY . /app`), `report.txt`, `secrets.env` and `raw/ice-dump.bin` (40 MB).
hints: `COPY .` sends everything in the build context into the image. A file named `.dockerignore` next to the Dockerfile tells Docker what to leave out of the context entirely.
`.dockerignore` lists one pattern per line, like a `.gitignore`. Name the credentials file and the data folder, then rebuild with `docker build -t NAME:TAG .`.

```bash
printf 'secrets.env\nraw\n' > .dockerignore
docker build -t kestrel/outbound:1.0 .
docker run --rm kestrel/outbound:1.0 ls /app
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
WORKDIR /app
COPY . /app
CMD ["cat", "/app/report.txt"]
Kestrel Point weekly report: ice cores logged 14, generators nominal, morale cautious.

MAINLAND_API_KEY=kp-live-93f1c0a7
MAINLAND_PASSWORD=hunter-two

validation.description: The image contains `report.txt` but no `secrets.env` and no `raw` folder

missions.debrief: `.dockerignore` filters the build context before anything is sent to the builder, so excluded files cannot leak into any layer and builds get faster. Pro tip: ignore `.git`, `*.env` and bulk data by default in every project.

missions.title: Travel Light
missions.story:
BUILD LOG, tidegauge, Amara's laptop:

  Step 1/4 : FROM golang:1.23-alpine
  Successfully tagged kestrel/tidegauge:0.1
  REPOSITORY         TAG   SIZE
  kestrel/tidegauge  0.1   318MB

The tide gauge reader is a 30-line Go program, but the image ships the entire Go toolchain with it. Rafael will carry it over a metered satellite link, and 318 MB for one tiny tool is absurd.

Build `kestrel/tidegauge:1.0` in two stages: compile with `golang:1.23-alpine`, then ship only the binary on `alpine:3.20`. It must come in under 25 MB and carry no Go toolchain.
objectives: Write a multi-stage `/workspace/Dockerfile`: build stage on `golang:1.23-alpine`, final stage on `alpine:3.20`
Build `kestrel/tidegauge:1.0` (under 25 MB) whose default command prints the tide reading
The final image must not contain the `go` toolchain
missions.startingState: `/workspace` holds `main.go` and `go.mod` for the tide gauge reader. There is no Dockerfile.
hints: A Dockerfile can contain several `FROM` lines. Each starts a new stage, and only the last stage becomes the final image, so build tools can live in an earlier stage and be left behind.
Name the first stage with `FROM ... AS build`, compile there with `go build`, then in the final stage use `COPY --from=build` to take just the binary. Setting `CGO_ENABLED=0` yields a static binary.

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'

missions.title: Ghost in the Layers
missions.story:
From: Tomasz Wierzba
Subject: URGENT, a password I deleted is still there

The legacy image `kestrel/legacy-archive:0.9` was built years ago. Its Dockerfile copied in a credentials file and then ran `rm` on it in the next step, so I assumed the password was gone. Wren's predecessor says it is not. Prove it.

Recover the archive password from the image's layers and write it to `/workspace/recovered.txt`. The original source folder was deleted, so you only have the image. Then build a clean `kestrel/archive-clean:1.0` from `alpine:3.20` that ships `/workspace/index.txt` as `/srv/archive/index.txt`, with no trace of the password in any layer.
objectives: Recover the archive password (the `ARCHIVE_PASSWORD` value) from the layers of `kestrel/legacy-archive:0.9` and write it to `/workspace/recovered.txt`
Build `kestrel/archive-clean:1.0` from `alpine:3.20` that contains `/srv/archive/index.txt`
The clean image must have no password file and no trace of the password in its history
missions.startingState: The image `kestrel/legacy-archive:0.9` exists locally. `/workspace/index.txt` is the new archive index. The old build folder no longer exists.
hints: A deleted file is only hidden by a newer layer. The earlier layer that added it is still stored inside the image, and `docker history` lists the steps that created each layer.

Export the image with `docker save IMAGE -o file.tar` and unpack it with `tar`. Every layer is a gzipped tarball under `blobs/`; list their contents with `tar -tzf` until you find the file that `docker history` shows being copied in, then extract just that file to stdout. For the clean image, never copy the credentials file in at all.

```bash
docker history --no-trunc kestrel/legacy-archive:0.9
docker save kestrel/legacy-archive:0.9 -o legacy.tar
mkdir -p x && tar -xf legacy.tar -C x
for b in x/blobs/sha256/*; do tar -tzf $b 2>/dev/null | grep -q archive.cred && tar -xzOf $b etc/archive.cred; done
# write the password value to recovered.txt, then build an image from FROM + COPY index.txt only
```

mkdir -p /tmp/legacy-build && cd /tmp/legacy-build && printf 'ARCHIVE_PASSWORD=Borealis-7714-Tern
' > archive.cred && printf 'FROM alpine:3.20
COPY archive.cred /etc/archive.cred
RUN rm /etc/archive.cred
CMD ["echo", "archive ready"]
' > Dockerfile && docker build -q -t kestrel/legacy-archive:0.9 . && cd / && rm -rf /tmp/legacy-build

missions.title: Names on the Wire
missions.story:
NORA: WEATHER-CACHE UNREACHABLE. FORECASTER LOOKUP FAILED: HOST NOT FOUND.
NORA: RETRY 41 OF 41. GIVING UP.

Amara Okafor left a note under the alert. The forecaster hard-codes the cache's IP address, and that address changes every time the cache restarts. "Give them a network where names just work," the note says. "The default bridge will not."

Build the wire: a network called `station-net`, a Redis cache named `weather-cache`, and a `forecaster` container that can reach the cache by its name.
objectives: Create a user-defined bridge network named `station-net`
Run `weather-cache` from `redis:7-alpine` on `station-net`
Run `forecaster` from `alpine:3.20` (kept alive with `sleep infinity`) on `station-net`
From inside `forecaster`, `ping weather-cache` must succeed
missions.startingState: A clean engine: no custom networks and no containers. The forecaster's config still says the cache host is `weather-cache`.
hints: Containers on the default bridge cannot resolve each other by name. A network you create yourself has built-in DNS. Look at the `docker network` command family.
Create the network with `docker network create <name>`, then attach each container at start time with `docker run --network <name> ...`. The container name is the DNS name.

```bash
docker network create station-net
docker run -d --name weather-cache --network station-net redis:7-alpine
docker run -d --name forecaster --network station-net alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker exec forecaster ping -c 1 weather-cache
```

CACHE_HOST=weather-cache
CACHE_PORT=6379

validation.description: Network `station-net` exists and uses the bridge driver
Inside `forecaster`, the name `weather-cache` resolves and answers a ping

solution: docker run -d --name forecaster --network station-net alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
missions.debrief: On a user-defined network Docker runs an embedded DNS server, so every container is reachable by its name and IPs stop mattering. Pro tip: put each group of cooperating services on its own network instead of sharing the default bridge.

missions.title: Answer to an Old Name
missions.story:
From: Tomasz Wierzba
Subject: The archive has moved, the scripts have not

Every 2019 field script fetches `http://archive/`. That machine no longer exists. Amara's replacement is called `archive-v2`, and I will not edit forty scripts by hand: one typo and a season of readings lands in the wrong place.

The network `legacy-net` already exists and `old-script` is running on it, still asking for the old name. Start `archive-v2` on that network so that the name `archive` reaches it. Confirm before the evening shift. I would like to sleep.
objectives: Run `archive-v2` from `nginx:alpine` on the network `legacy-net`
Give `archive-v2` the network alias `archive` on `legacy-net`
From inside `old-script`, `http://archive/` must return the archive's web page
missions.startingState: Network `legacy-net` exists and container `old-script` (alpine) is running on it. Nothing answers to `archive` yet.
hints: A container can carry extra DNS names on a network besides its own name. Check the options of `docker run` that mention the network.
Use `--network legacy-net` together with `--network-alias <name>`. The alias only exists on the network it was given for.

```bash
docker run -d --name archive-v2 \
  --network legacy-net --network-alias archive \
  nginx:alpine
docker exec old-script wget -qO- http://archive/
```

commands: docker run -d --name old-script --network legacy-net alpine:3.20 sleep infinity

validation.description: `old-script` can fetch `http://archive/` and gets the nginx page

solution: docker run -d --name archive-v2 --network legacy-net --network-alias archive nginx:alpine
missions.debrief: Old scripts keep working because the new container answers to the old hostname, and nobody had to touch a single client. Pro tip: aliases belong to one network, so the same container can go by different names on different networks.

missions.title: Moving Day for the Printer
missions.story:
A sticky note on the lab printer, in marker: "DO NOT UNPLUG. Halfway through printing the whole winter duty roster, 212 pages. Kip."

Underneath, in Ingrid Halvorsen's handwriting: "The printer is the container `lab-printer`, and it still sits on the default bridge where nobody can find it by name. The lab machines live on `lab-net`. Move it. If the container restarts, the job restarts at page 1 and we lose the evening."

Put `lab-printer` on `lab-net` and take it off the default bridge, without restarting it.
objectives: `lab-printer` is attached to `lab-net`
`lab-printer` is no longer attached to the default `bridge` network
`lab-desk` can ping `lab-printer` by name
The print job survives: `/spool/job-started` inside `lab-printer` must still exist (no restart)
missions.startingState: Container `lab-printer` runs on the default bridge with a print job in its RAM spool. `lab-net` exists with `lab-desk` on it.
hints: A running container can be attached to and detached from networks without stopping it. Both actions live under `docker network`.
`docker network connect <network> <container>` adds a network, `docker network disconnect <network> <container>` removes one. The default network is literally named `bridge`.

```bash
docker network connect lab-net lab-printer
docker network disconnect bridge lab-printer
docker inspect -f '{{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}' lab-printer
```

commands: docker run -d --name lab-desk --network lab-net alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker run -d --name lab-printer --tmpfs /spool alpine:3.20 sh -c 'date +%s > /spool/job-started; sleep infinity'

validation.description: `lab-printer` is no longer on the default `bridge` network
The print job is intact: `/spool/job-started` still exists, so the container was never restarted

missions.debrief: Networks can be attached and detached while a container keeps running, so topology changes do not need downtime. Pro tip: connect to the new network before disconnecting from the old one so there is never a moment without a route.

missions.title: The Sealed Vault
missions.story:
SEED VAULT COMMISSIONING CHECKLIST (Ingrid Halvorsen)
[x] Service image chosen: nginx:alpine
[x] Freezer room power confirmed
[ ] Network: sealed. No route to the mainland, the satellite link or the crew wifi. If anything inside is ever compromised, it must not be able to call home.
[ ] Service running as `seed-vault`

Two boxes are still open, and the vault holds the only copy of the station's seed collection. Create an internal network called `vault-net`, then run `seed-vault` on it and nowhere else. Prove it cannot reach the internet.
objectives: Create the network `vault-net` as an internal network
Run `seed-vault` from `nginx:alpine` on `vault-net`
`seed-vault` must not be attached to the default `bridge` network
An outbound request from inside `seed-vault` to `1.1.1.1` must fail
missions.startingState: A clean engine. Nothing has been created for the vault yet.
hints: Networks can be created with no gateway to the outside world. Look for a flag on `docker network create` that says the network is internal.
Create the network with `--internal`, then start the container with `--network vault-net` only. Attaching a second, normal network would give it a route out again.

```bash
docker network create --internal vault-net
docker run -d --name seed-vault --network vault-net nginx:alpine
docker exec seed-vault wget -T 3 -qO- http://1.1.1.1
```

validation.description: `seed-vault` is not attached to the default `bridge` network
A request from `seed-vault` to `http://1.1.1.1` fails (no route out)

missions.debrief: An internal network lets containers talk to each other but removes the gateway, so nothing on it can reach outside. Pro tip: a container attached to both an internal and a normal network is still exposed, so check `docker inspect` for stray attachments.

missions.title: Admin Eyes Only
missions.story:
[RADIO] Kestrel Control, this is Halvorsen. Kip ran a port scan from the crew wifi and found the admin panel on port 9090, wide open to anybody on the station network. It has the door controls and the generator schedule on it. Kip says it "looked like a printer".

The panel is the container `admin-panel`, started last week with a plain `-p 9090:80`. Only a shell on the control machine itself should reach it. Recreate it with the same page and the same read-only mount, but with port 9090 listening on loopback only. Confirm from your side. Halvorsen out.
objectives: Run `admin-panel` from `nginx:alpine` with `/workspace/panel` mounted read-only at `/usr/share/nginx/html`
Publish container port 80 on `127.0.0.1:9090` only (not on `0.0.0.0`)
`http://127.0.0.1:9090/` from the control machine still serves the admin console page
missions.startingState: `admin-panel` is already running but published on every interface (`0.0.0.0:9090`). Its page is in `/workspace/panel`.
hints: A published port can be tied to one host address. The address goes in front of the port numbers in the publish option. A running container's ports cannot be edited, so you will recreate it.
The `-p` syntax is `[host-ip:]host-port:container-port`. Remove the old container first, then start a new one with the same name, the same bind mount and a loopback host-ip.

```bash
docker rm -f admin-panel
docker run -d --name admin-panel \
  -p 127.0.0.1:9090:80 \
  -v /workspace/panel:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro \
  nginx:alpine
docker port admin-panel
```

files.content:
KESTREL ADMIN CONSOLE

Doors, generators, heating.

missions.debrief: Publishing with `-p 9090:80` means every interface; adding a host IP such as `127.0.0.1` narrows who can connect. Pro tip: `docker port <name>` shows the real bindings, which is the quickest way to audit exposure.

missions.title: Isolation Chamber
missions.story:
03:12:07 NORA  CALIBRATOR: NET LINK UP (eth0 172.17.0.3)
03:12:09 NORA  CALIBRATOR: CONTACTING telemetry.example.org
03:12:09 NORA  WARNING: SENSOR BASELINE MAY BE CONTAMINATED
03:12:44 NORA  BENCH-MONITOR: CANNOT SEE docker0 OR ANY STATION NIC

Amara Okafor's calibration run must happen with no network at all: every packet it sends spoils the baseline. The new `bench-monitor` has the opposite job. It watches the station's real network cards, so it needs to see the engine host's network stack, not a private one.

Replace `calibrator` with a fully offline container, and start `bench-monitor` sharing the host's network.
objectives: `calibrator` (`alpine:3.20`) is running with the network mode `none` (no `eth0`)
`bench-monitor` (`alpine:3.20`) is running with the network mode `host`
Inside `bench-monitor` the host interface `docker0` is visible
missions.startingState: A `calibrator` container is running on the default bridge, so it still has network access. `bench-monitor` does not exist.
hints: Besides user-defined networks, a container can run with no networking at all or share the host's stack. Both are chosen with the same `docker run` option. The mode of an existing container cannot be changed.
Use `--network none` for the offline container and `--network host` for the one that must see the host's interfaces. Remove the old `calibrator` first, since its name is taken.

```bash
docker rm -f calibrator
docker run -d --name calibrator --network none alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker run -d --name bench-monitor --network host alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker exec calibrator ls /sys/class/net
docker exec bench-monitor ls /sys/class/net
```

commands: docker run -d --name calibrator alpine:3.20 sleep infinity

solution: docker run -d --name calibrator --network none alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker run -d --name bench-monitor --network host alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
missions.debrief: `--network none` leaves only a loopback interface, while `--network host` removes network isolation completely. Pro tip: host mode skips port publishing, so anything it listens on is directly exposed on the host.

missions.title: Fixed Addresses
missions.story:
#kestrel-ops
Amara: the 2011 sensor firmware has the collector's addresses burned in. no DNS, no config, just numbers
Kip: so can we just change the numbers?
Amara: it is flashed on 31 sensors, on a glacier, Kip.

The addresses the emulated sensors must answer on are in `legacy/sensors.conf`. Build a network called `sensor-grid` on the subnet from that file and start the three sensors (nginx stand-ins) so each sits on its burned-in address. A `collector` container must be able to fetch each sensor's page by IP.
objectives: Create the network `sensor-grid` with the subnet listed in `/workspace/legacy/sensors.conf`
Run `sensor-07`, `sensor-12` and `sensor-31` from `nginx:alpine` on `sensor-grid` with the IPs from that file
Run `collector` from `alpine:3.20` on `sensor-grid`
From inside `collector`, `http://172.28.0.31/` must answer
missions.startingState: `/workspace/legacy/sensors.conf` lists the subnet and the three addresses. No networks or containers exist yet.
hints: Docker normally picks addresses for you. To control them you need to define the network's address range yourself and then ask for a specific address when you start each container. Read the config file first.
`docker network create --subnet <cidr> <name>` fixes the range; `docker run --network <name> --ip <addr>` requests an address inside it. `--ip` only works on user-defined networks that have a subnet.

```bash
cat legacy/sensors.conf
docker network create --subnet 172.28.0.0/24 sensor-grid
docker run -d --name sensor-07 --network sensor-grid --ip 172.28.0.7 nginx:alpine
# ...repeat for sensor-12 and sensor-31, then:
docker run -d --name collector --network sensor-grid alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker exec collector wget -qO- http://172.28.0.7/
```

SUBNET=172.28.0.0/24
sensor-07=172.28.0.7
sensor-12=172.28.0.12
sensor-31=172.28.0.31

solution: docker run -d --name collector --network sensor-grid alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
missions.debrief: Static addressing needs a network you control: define the subnet first, then pin containers to addresses inside it. Pro tip: keep fixed addresses out of the range Docker hands out automatically (`--ip-range`) so a random container never grabs one first.

modules.title: Ice-Core Archive
modules.theme: Make the data outlive containers, upgrades and winter

missions.title: Cores Outlive Containers
missions.story:
From: Tomasz Wierzba
Subject: Eleven days of readings, gone

The core logger kept eleven days of depth readings inside its own container. Tuesday's upgrade replaced that container, and the readings went with it. I am not going to describe how that felt.

Before I trust the new setup, I need proof. From a throwaway container called `core-logger`, write the depth reading of core 0417 into a volume named `ice-cores`. Then delete the container. The reading must still be there afterwards.
objectives: Create a named volume `ice-cores` and mount it at `/data` in a container named `core-logger` (`alpine:3.20`)
Write `DEPTH 1450 M` into the file `/data/core-0417.txt`
Remove the `core-logger` container
The volume `ice-cores` must still hold `core-0417.txt`
missions.startingState: A clean engine: no volumes and no containers.
hints: Anything written in a container's own filesystem is deleted with the container. A named volume is stored separately and outlives it.
Mount the volume with `-v ice-cores:/data` (it is created if missing). Run a one-shot command that writes the file, then remove the container with `docker rm`.

```bash
docker run --name core-logger -v ice-cores:/data alpine:3.20 \
  sh -c 'echo "DEPTH 1450 M" > /data/core-0417.txt'
docker rm core-logger
docker run --rm -v ice-cores:/data alpine:3.20 cat /data/core-0417.txt
```

validation.description: A fresh container mounting `ice-cores` can still read `core-0417.txt` containing `DEPTH 1450 M`

solution: docker run --name core-logger -v ice-cores:/data alpine:3.20 sh -c 'echo "DEPTH 1450 M" > /data/core-0417.txt'
missions.debrief: A named volume lives under the engine's control, independent of any container, so removing the container leaves the data alone. Pro tip: `docker rm -v` only removes anonymous volumes; named ones are never deleted unless you run `docker volume rm`.

missions.title: The Field Journal
missions.story:
Pinned to the mess-hall corkboard, in Kip Lindqvist's loopy handwriting:

"Everyone writes the daily field journal into /workspace/journal and Tomasz wants it as a website. I made one, but I copied the files INTO the image, so every new entry needs a rebuild. Also I once typed into it from inside the container. Help??"

Serve the journal with nginx as `field-journal` on port 8085. The folder must be mounted, not copied, so new entries appear at once, and mounted read-only so the website can never alter an entry.
objectives: Run `field-journal` from `nginx:alpine` publishing port `8085` to container port 80
Bind-mount `/workspace/journal` at `/usr/share/nginx/html` read-only
`http://localhost:8085/day-02.txt` returns the journal entry
Writing into `/usr/share/nginx/html` inside the container must fail
missions.startingState: The folder `/workspace/journal` holds three daily entries (`day-01.txt` to `day-03.txt`). No containers are running.
hints: A bind mount maps a host directory into a container, so edits on one side show up on the other immediately. You can also mark the mount so the container cannot write to it.
Use `-v <absolute-host-path>:<container-path>:ro` together with `-p 8085:80`. nginx serves files from `/usr/share/nginx/html`.

```bash
docker run -d --name field-journal -p 8085:80 \
  -v /workspace/journal:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro \
  nginx:alpine
curl http://localhost:8085/day-02.txt
```

DAY 02 - Core drill assembled. Tomasz counted the bolts twice.
DAY 03 - First 40 metres of ice recovered. Generator coughing again.

validation.description: Writing into the mounted folder fails inside the container

missions.debrief: Edits in `/workspace/journal` appear instantly because the container reads the host folder directly, and `:ro` keeps it a pure reader. Pro tip: bind mounts need an absolute host path; a bare name like `journal` silently creates a named volume instead.

missions.title: Scratch Paper
missions.story:
decoder[1]: writing /scratch/frame.tmp (412 MB)
decoder[1]: writing /scratch/frame.tmp (412 MB)
kernel: overlayfs: no space left on device
NORA: DISK 98 PERCENT. SNAPSHOT JOB ABORTED.

Amara Okafor's signal decoder dumps huge throwaway frames every minute. Overnight they filled the disk that holds the station's snapshots. Temporary files belong in RAM, and the amount should be capped so a runaway decoder cannot eat the machine's memory either.

The script is in `/workspace/decoder`. It refuses to start unless `/scratch` is RAM-backed.
objectives: Run `decoder` from `alpine:3.20` with the command `sh /opt/decoder/decode.sh`
Bind-mount `/workspace/decoder` at `/opt/decoder` (read-only is fine)
Mount a `tmpfs` at `/scratch` limited to 16 MB
The decoder's logs must show that it started and wrote its frame
missions.startingState: `/workspace/decoder/decode.sh` exists. No containers are running.
hints: Docker can mount an in-memory filesystem into a container; nothing is written to disk and it disappears when the container stops. This is a `docker run` option, and it takes a size parameter.
Use `--tmpfs /scratch:rw,size=16m` for the RAM mount and `-v /workspace/decoder:/opt/decoder:ro` to bring in the script. Then give the command `sh /opt/decoder/decode.sh`.

```bash
docker run -d --name decoder \
  --tmpfs /scratch:rw,size=16m \
  -v /workspace/decoder:/opt/decoder:ro \
  alpine:3.20 sh /opt/decoder/decode.sh
docker logs decoder
```

files.content:
#!/bin/sh
if ! grep -q ' /scratch tmpfs ' /proc/mounts; then
  echo "REFUSING TO START: /scratch is not RAM-backed" >&2
  exit 3
fi
echo "frame-0001" > /scratch/frame.tmp
echo "SCRATCH IS RAM: decoder ready"
exec sleep infinity

validation.description: The decoder reports `SCRATCH IS RAM` in its logs

missions.debrief: Nothing written to `/scratch` ever reaches the disk: tmpfs lives in RAM and disappears with the container. Pro tip: always cap it with `size=`, or a runaway decoder can eat the memory your other services need.

missions.title: Pack for the Ship
missions.story:
[RADIO] Petrel to Kestrel Point, Duarte here. We sail at dawn and the weather does not wait for paperwork. Tomasz wants the seismograph data on the mainland tonight, and the satellite link is not carrying that much. Put it in a single tarball in `/workspace/backups` and I will collect it from the dock.

The data lives in the volume `seismo-data`, and no container is using it right now. Create `/workspace/backups/seismo.tar.gz` holding the volume's files, using a throwaway container that mounts both the volume and the backups folder. Leave the volume as it is. Duarte out.
objectives: Create the archive `/workspace/backups/seismo.tar.gz` (gzip-compressed tar)
It must contain the files of the volume `seismo-data`, including `readings-2026.csv` and `stations/north.csv`
Use a throwaway container (for example `alpine:3.20`) that mounts the volume and `/workspace/backups`
The volume `seismo-data` must still exist
missions.startingState: The volume `seismo-data` already holds seismograph readings. The folder `/workspace/backups` does not exist yet.
hints: A volume has no file path on your shell, so to copy it out you run a helper container that mounts the volume and a host folder together, and let `tar` do the packing inside it.
Mount the volume at `/data` and a bind mount of `/workspace/backups` at `/backup`, then run `tar czf /backup/seismo.tar.gz -C /data .`. Add `--rm` so the helper disappears.

```bash
mkdir -p backups
docker run --rm \
  -v seismo-data:/data \
  -v /workspace/backups:/backup \
  alpine:3.20 tar czf /backup/seismo.tar.gz -C /data .
tar tzf backups/seismo.tar.gz
```

docker run --rm -v seismo-data:/data alpine:3.20 sh -c 'mkdir -p /data/stations && printf "time,amplitude
00:00,0.12
00:01,0.15
" > /data/readings-2026.csv && printf "north,71.2,-8.4
" > /data/stations/north.csv'

missions.debrief: Volumes have no export button; the trick is a throwaway helper container that mounts both the volume and a host folder and archives one into the other. Pro tip: `tar -C /data .` stores relative paths, so the archive restores cleanly anywhere.

missions.title: Unpack the Delivery
missions.story:
Tomasz: The Petrel delivered `glacier.tar.gz` from the mainland lab. Forty years of glacier-front measurements.
Ingrid: Where is it?
Tomasz: In `/workspace/incoming`. I cannot simply extract it on the host. The permissions on the old server were a swamp, and the viewer containers expect it in a Docker volume.

Ingrid: Then make it a volume, engineer. There is a `MANIFEST.sha256` inside. Nobody tells Tomasz it is done until the checksums pass.
objectives: Create a new volume named `glacier-data`
Extract `/workspace/incoming/glacier.tar.gz` into it using a throwaway container (the tarball must stay in place)
`sha256sum -c MANIFEST.sha256` inside the volume must report every file `OK`
missions.startingState: The tarball `/workspace/incoming/glacier.tar.gz` exists. No volume called `glacier-data` exists yet.
hints: Restoring is the reverse of backing up: a helper container mounts the target volume and the folder with the tarball, and unpacks one into the other.
Mount the volume at `/data` and `/workspace/incoming` at `/incoming` (read-only is fine), then run `tar xzf /incoming/glacier.tar.gz -C /data`.

  -v /workspace/incoming:/incoming:ro \
  alpine:3.20 tar xzf /incoming/glacier.tar.gz -C /data
docker run --rm -v glacier-data:/data alpine:3.20 \
  sh -c 'cd /data && sha256sum -c MANIFEST.sha256'
```

missions.title: One Writer, Many Readers
missions.story:
NORA: TELEMETRY FEED CORRUPTED 04:12. CAUSE: reader-ops OPENED latest.txt FOR WRITING.
NORA: THIS HAS HAPPENED BEFORE.
NORA: NOBODY LISTENS TO NORA.

The telemetry feed has exactly one writer, `producer`, and two consumers: the ops desk and the lab. Last night a reader script wrote into the shared volume and wrecked the feed. The new rule is that readers may look but never touch.

Build it: a volume `telemetry`; `producer` writes a fresh `tick <timestamp>` line to `/data/latest.txt` every second; `reader-ops` and `reader-lab` see the same volume at `/feed`, strictly read-only.
objectives: Run `producer` (`alpine:3.20`) with the volume `telemetry` mounted read-write at `/data`, rewriting `/data/latest.txt` with `tick <timestamp>` every second
Run `reader-ops` and `reader-lab` (`alpine:3.20`, `sleep infinity`) with the same volume mounted at `/feed` read-only
A reader can read `/feed/latest.txt` but any write under `/feed` fails
missions.startingState: A clean engine: no volume `telemetry` and no containers.
hints: Several containers can mount the same named volume at the same time. Each mount has its own mode, so the writer and the readers can have different permissions on the same data.
Add `:ro` to the readers' mount: `-v telemetry:/feed:ro`. For the writer, run a shell loop: `sh -c 'while true; do echo "tick $(date +%s)" > /data/latest.txt; sleep 1; done'`.

```bash
docker volume create telemetry
docker run -d --name producer -v telemetry:/data alpine:3.20 \
  sh -c 'while true; do echo "tick $(date +%s)" > /data/latest.txt; sleep 1; done'
docker run -d --name reader-ops -v telemetry:/feed:ro alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker run -d --name reader-lab -v telemetry:/feed:ro alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker exec reader-ops touch /feed/x   # must fail
```

validation.description: `reader-lab` can read the producer's `tick` line from `/feed/latest.txt`

solution: docker run -d --name producer -v telemetry:/data alpine:3.20 sh -c 'while true; do echo "tick $(date +%s)" > /data/latest.txt; sleep 1; done'
docker run -d --name reader-ops -v telemetry:/feed:ro alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker run -d --name reader-lab -v telemetry:/feed:ro alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
missions.debrief: One volume can be mounted many times, and each mount has its own access mode, so a single trusted writer can feed any number of read-only consumers. Pro tip: grant `:ro` by default and give write access only to the one container that truly needs it.

missions.title: Write It Down Once
missions.story:
Taped to the rack, in Tomasz's tiny handwriting:

"After every power blip I retype the same docker run line from memory. Last night I got the port wrong and the crew stared at a blank dashboard until breakfast.

Ingrid says the whole station should live in ONE file. Start with the dashboard. `restart-dashboard.sh` shows what I type; the hand-started container `dashboard-hand` is still sitting on port 8090. Please replace it with a Compose project named `station`, so one command brings the dashboard back every time. -- T.W."
objectives: Remove the hand-started container `dashboard-hand`
Create `/workspace/compose.yaml` with the top-level project name `station`
Define a service `dashboard` from `nginx:alpine`, publishing host port 8090 to container port 80 and mounting `./dashboard` read-only at `/usr/share/nginx/html`
Bring the project up in the background so http://localhost:8090 shows the dashboard
missions.startingState: `/workspace/dashboard/index.html` and Tomasz's `restart-dashboard.sh` exist; container `dashboard-hand` is already serving the page on port 8090.
hints: Compose lets you describe containers in a YAML file instead of typing `docker run` flags. The file is called `compose.yaml`, and a single `docker compose` command in that folder reads it. Port 8090 is taken, so deal with the old container first.

The file has two top-level keys: `name:` (the project name) and `services:`. Under a service you list `image`, a `ports` list written as "host:container", and `volumes` where a trailing `:ro` makes the mount read-only. Remove the old container with `docker rm -f`, then start the project with `docker compose up -d`.

Put this in `compose.yaml`, then run `docker rm -f dashboard-hand && docker compose up -d`:

```yaml
name: station
services:
  dashboard:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8090:80"
    volumes:
      - ./dashboard:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro
```

files.content:
KESTREL DASHBOARD

Power: nominal. Wind: 41 km/h. Ice: stable.

#!/bin/sh

docker rm -f dashboard-hand
docker run -d --name dashboard-hand -p 8090:80 \
  -v /workspace/dashboard:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro nginx:alpine

validation.description: Compose project `station` has a running `dashboard` service
The dashboard content is mounted read-only at `/usr/share/nginx/html`

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: station
services:
  dashboard:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8090:80"
    volumes:
      - ./dashboard:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro
EOF
missions.debrief: A compose.yaml turns a pile of remembered flags into a file you can read, review and version: `docker compose up -d` always rebuilds the same state, and the `name:` key decides which project owns the containers. Pro tip: `docker compose config` prints the fully resolved file, which is the fastest way to catch YAML mistakes before anything starts.

missions.title: Two Services, One File
missions.story:
**#kestrel-dev, 02:14**

Amara: the hit counter works on my laptop!!

Amara: it needs redis. `app/app.py` reads `REDIS_HOST` from the environment. I was running redis in a tmux pane. don't ask.

Amara: can you put both in one compose file? project name `weather-desk`. the API is `api` on port 8100, redis is `cache`, and api shouldn't start before cache exists. I'm going to sleep.
objectives: Create `/workspace/compose.yaml` for the project `weather-desk`
Service `cache` runs `redis:7-alpine`
Service `api` runs `python:3.12-alpine` with command `python /app/app.py`, mounts `./app` at `/app` read-only, publishes 8100 to 8000, sets `REDIS_HOST=cache` and declares `depends_on: cache`
Start the project so http://localhost:8100 returns the hit counter
missions.startingState: `/workspace/app/app.py` is Amara's counter service; nothing is running yet.
hints: Both programs go into one `compose.yaml` under `services:`. Services on the same Compose project can reach each other by service name, so the API only needs the right hostname handed to it as an environment variable.

Give `api` an `environment:` block whose value is the name of the redis service, and a `depends_on:` list so Compose starts `cache` first. Because the code lives in `./app`, mount that folder and set `command:` to run the script from the mounted path.

A full file for this mission looks like this. Save it as `compose.yaml` and run `docker compose up -d`:

```yaml
name: weather-desk
services:
  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
  api:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: python /app/app.py
    volumes:
      - ./app:/app:ro
    ports:
      - "8100:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: cache
    depends_on:
      - cache
```

files.content:
import os, socket
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

HOST = os.environ["REDIS_HOST"]


def bump():
    with socket.create_connection((HOST, 6379), timeout=2) as s:
        s.sendall(b"INCR hits\r\n")
        return int(s.recv(64).strip()[1:])


class Desk(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        body = f"WEATHER DESK hits={bump()}\n".encode()
        self.send_response(200)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)


HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), Desk).serve_forever()

params.command: docker compose -p weather-desk exec -T api printenv REDIS_HOST

validation.description: http://localhost:8100 returns the hit counter from redis

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: weather-desk
services:
  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
  api:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: python /app/app.py
    volumes:
      - ./app:/app:ro
    ports:
      - "8100:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: cache
    depends_on:
      - cache
EOF
missions.debrief: Compose gives every project its own network where each service name is a DNS name, so `REDIS_HOST: cache` is all the wiring the API needs. Pro tip: `depends_on` only orders container start, not readiness -- if the dependency needs time to become usable, pair it with a healthcheck.

missions.title: Build on Arrival
missions.story:
```
[nightly] 03:00:01 docker build -t ingest-dev ./ingest      OK
[nightly] 03:00:09 docker run -d -p 8110:8000 kestrel/ingest:dev

She wants build and run to stop disagreeing: a Compose project `ingest-bay` with one service `ingest`, built from the `./ingest` folder and tagged `kestrel/ingest:dev`.
objectives: Create `/workspace/compose.yaml` for project `ingest-bay`
Service `ingest` builds from `./ingest` and is tagged `kestrel/ingest:dev`
It publishes host port 8110 to container port 8000
Run it so image `kestrel/ingest:dev` exists and http://localhost:8110 answers

hints: A Compose service can carry a `build:` instruction instead of only pulling an image, so Compose builds it for you during `up`. If the service also has an `image:` key, that key becomes the name the built image receives.
Under the service use `build: ./ingest` (the folder containing the Dockerfile) together with `image: kestrel/ingest:dev`. Then `docker compose up -d --build` builds and starts it in one go.

missions.title: Wait for the Database
missions.story:
[RADIO -- PETREL, CHANNEL 9]

Rafael Duarte: Kestrel Point, Petrel. I sail at dawn and my cargo manifest has to be in your database before I load. Last time the migration ran while Postgres was still starting, the table never got made, and I loaded half the crates blind. Over.

Ingrid, from the doorway: Compose project `manifest`, engineer. Service `db` is Postgres, container name `manifest-db`, with a health check. Service `migrate` runs `migrations/001_cargo.sql` once the database is healthy, then exits cleanly. The tide won't wait. Over.
objectives: Create `/workspace/compose.yaml` for project `manifest`
Service `db` runs `postgres:16-alpine` with `container_name: manifest-db`, a `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, and a healthcheck
Service `migrate` runs `psql` against host `db` with the file `/migrations/001_cargo.sql` (mount `./migrations`), starts only when `db` is healthy and exits with code 0
Bring the project up: `manifest-db` is healthy and table `cargo_manifest` contains 3 rows
missions.startingState: `/workspace/migrations/001_cargo.sql` creates and fills `cargo_manifest`; there is no compose file yet.
hints: A container being 'started' is not the same as the service inside it being ready. Compose can wait for a health check: give `db` a `healthcheck`, and make `migrate` depend on it with a condition rather than just a name.

Use `pg_isready` as the health test and `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy` on the migrator. The migrator can reuse the Postgres image just for its `psql` client; give it `PGPASSWORD` and set `restart: "no"` so it exits once and stays done. Use `-h 127.0.0.1` in the health test so it only turns healthy when Postgres accepts network connections.

A complete file, followed by `docker compose up -d`:

```yaml
name: manifest
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    container_name: manifest-db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: kestrel-pass
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
  migrate:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: kestrel-pass
    volumes:
      - ./migrations:/migrations:ro
    command: ["psql", "-h", "db", "-U", "postgres", "-v", "ON_ERROR_STOP=1", "-f", "/migrations/001_cargo.sql"]
    restart: "no"
```

validation.description: The one-shot `migrate` container finished with exit code 0

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: manifest
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    container_name: manifest-db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: kestrel-pass
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
  migrate:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: kestrel-pass
    volumes:
      - ./migrations:/migrations:ro
    command: ["psql", "-h", "db", "-U", "postgres", "-v", "ON_ERROR_STOP=1", "-f", "/migrations/001_cargo.sql"]
    restart: "no"
EOF
missions.debrief: `condition: service_healthy` makes the migrator wait for the moment the database actually answers, not just the moment its process starts. Pro tip: write migrations with `IF NOT EXISTS`, so rerunning the one-shot service is harmless.

missions.title: Many Hands
missions.story:
NORA: SURVEY-QUEUE BACKLOG 412 JOBS
NORA: SURVEY-WORKER COUNT 1. EXPECTED 3
NORA: CPU HEADROOM 71 PERCENT. IDLE

The glacier survey pipeline (Compose project `survey`) has a `queue` and a single `worker`. The jobs are independent; three workers would clear the backlog before the shift ends. Amara tried to scale it and got a name conflict, because the compose file pins a container name and a host port on the worker. Fix the file so `docker compose up -d` leaves exactly three `worker` containers, and do not disturb the `queue`.
objectives: Edit `/workspace/compose.yaml` so service `worker` has no fixed `container_name` and no published host port
Project `survey` runs exactly 3 containers of service `worker` (via `deploy.replicas` or `--scale`)
Service `queue` keeps running
missions.startingState: Project `survey` is up with one `survey-worker` (host port 8200) and a redis `queue`.
hints: Compose names containers `project-service-N` so they can be numbered. A hard-coded `container_name` allows only one copy, and a fixed host port can be bound by only one container, so both must go before a service can have several replicas.

Delete the `container_name:` line and the `ports:` section from `worker`, then ask for three copies, either with `deploy: replicas: 3` in the file or with `docker compose up -d --scale worker=3` on the command line.

The worker section should end up like this, then run `docker compose up -d`:

```yaml
  worker:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"]
    deploy:
      replicas: 3
```

name: survey
services:
  queue:
    image: redis:7-alpine
  worker:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    container_name: survey-worker
    command: ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"]
    ports:
      - "8200:8000"

validation.description: `worker` no longer publishes fixed host port 8200
Exactly 3 `worker` containers are running in project `survey`

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: survey
services:
  queue:
    image: redis:7-alpine
  worker:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"]
    deploy:
      replicas: 3
EOF
missions.debrief: Anything that must be unique per container -- a fixed container name or a fixed host port -- blocks horizontal scaling; stateless workers should be anonymous and reached through the project network. Pro tip: `docker compose up -d --scale worker=5` changes the count on the fly, but `deploy.replicas` keeps the number written down in the file.

missions.title: Front Door, Back Room
missions.story:
FRONT-DOOR CHECKLIST -- Ingrid Halvorsen, unsigned

[ ] Crew traffic enters through `proxy` on port 8120 and nowhere else.
[ ] `db` lives in the back room: `proxy` must have no route to it, ever.
[ ] `api` is the only service allowed to stand in both rooms.

Right now all three services share one flat network, so a compromised proxy could talk straight to the database. Rework the stack in Compose project `frontdoor` with two networks, `front` and `back`, and bring it up again. Tick every box.
objectives: In `/workspace/compose.yaml` (project `frontdoor`) define networks `front` and `back`
`proxy` joins only `front`; `db` joins only `back`; `api` joins both
The stack runs, and http://localhost:8120 returns the API answer including `db=PONG`
From inside `proxy`, the hostname `db` must not resolve
missions.startingState: Project `frontdoor` runs with `proxy`, `api` and `db` all on Compose's default flat network.
hints: Compose creates one default network for a project, and every service on it can see every other. Containers can only resolve each other when they share at least one network, so segmentation means declaring your own networks and attaching each service only where it belongs.

Add a top-level `networks:` section with `front` and `back`, and a `networks:` list under every service. Once every service lists networks explicitly, the default one disappears. Then apply the change with `docker compose up -d`.

Keep the services you have and add the network wiring:

```yaml
services:
  proxy:
    networks: [front]
  api:
    networks: [front, back]
  db:
    networks: [back]
networks:
  front:
  back:
```

    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8120:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - api
  api:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["python", "/app/app.py"]
    volumes:
      - ./api:/app:ro
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
  db:
    image: redis:7-alpine

params.command: docker inspect -f '{{range $k,$v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}} {{end}}' $(docker ps -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=frontdoor --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=proxy) | xargs -n1 | sort | xargs

params.command: docker inspect -f '{{range $k,$v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}} {{end}}' $(docker ps -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=frontdoor --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=api) | xargs -n1 | sort | xargs

docker inspect -f '{{range $k,$v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}} {{end}}' $(docker ps -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=frontdoor --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=db) | xargs -n1 | sort | xargs

validation.description: `db` is attached only to the `back` network
The API can still reach the database through the proxy

params.command: docker compose -p frontdoor exec -T proxy sh -c 'getent hosts db || echo UNREACHABLE'

validation.description: From inside `proxy`, the name `db` does not resolve

solution:

name: frontdoor
services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8120:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - api
    networks: [front]
  api:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["python", "/app/app.py"]
    volumes:
      - ./api:/app:ro
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
    networks: [front, back]
  db:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    networks: [back]
networks:
  front:
  back:
EOF
missions.debrief: Multiple networks turn a flat 'everything talks to everything' layout into rooms with doors: only the service standing in both rooms can carry traffic between them. Pro tip: mark a network `internal: true` in Compose to also cut it off from the outside world.

missions.title: Settings Without Edits
missions.story:
**From:** Amara Okafor
**Subject:** lab-bench, again

Three people edited `compose.yaml` this week just to change a port, and Kip's `toolbox` debug container has been running on the bench for days eating CPU.

Please move the tunables into a `.env` file next to `compose.yaml`: `DESK_PORT=8130` and `DESK_TAG=1.27-alpine`, and make the `desk` service use them. `toolbox` should only exist when somebody asks for the `debug` profile. Project name stays `lab-bench`.

Thanks!! -- A.
objectives: Create `/workspace/.env` with `DESK_PORT=8130` and `DESK_TAG=1.27-alpine`
In `compose.yaml`, build the `desk` image name and host port from `${DESK_TAG}` and `${DESK_PORT}`
Put `toolbox` in the profile `debug`, and make sure no `toolbox` container is running
Project `lab-bench` serves http://localhost:8130 from `nginx:1.27-alpine`
missions.startingState: Project `lab-bench` is running with hard-coded values: `desk` on `nginx:alpine` (port 8000) and an always-on `toolbox`.
hints: Compose reads a file named `.env` in the project folder and substitutes `${VARIABLE}` references inside `compose.yaml`. Separately, a service can be tagged with `profiles`, which keeps it out of a plain `docker compose up` until that profile is requested.

In `.env` write one `KEY=value` per line. In the YAML use `nginx:${DESK_TAG}` and `"${DESK_PORT}:80"`, and add `profiles: ["debug"]` under `toolbox`. Editing the file does not stop the toolbox that is already running; remove it explicitly with `docker compose rm -sf toolbox`.

Put this into `.env`:

```bash
DESK_PORT=8130
DESK_TAG=1.27-alpine
```

and edit `compose.yaml` so it reads:

```yaml
name: lab-bench
services:
  desk:
    image: nginx:${DESK_TAG}
    ports:
      - "${DESK_PORT}:80"
  toolbox:
    image: alpine:3.20
    command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
    profiles: ["debug"]
```

Finish with `docker compose rm -sf toolbox` and `docker compose up -d`.

`compose.yaml` references `${DESK_TAG}` instead of a hard-coded tag
`toolbox` is only part of the project when the `debug` profile is requested

name: lab-bench
services:
  desk:
    image: nginx:${DESK_TAG}
