missions.debrief: Keeping tunables in `.env` means a port or tag change is a one-line edit that never touches the structure of the stack, and a profile keeps tools like a debug toolbox off until someone asks for them. Pro tip: `docker compose --profile debug up -d toolbox` starts it on demand, and `${VAR:-default}` supplies a fallback when the variable is missing.

modules.title: The Audit
modules.theme: An auditor arrives from the mainland: harden everything

missions.title: Nobody Runs as Root
missions.story:
AUDIT FINDING F-01
Auditor: Wren Achebe        Severity: HIGH

Observed: the process inside container `telemetry` runs as uid 0. A single bug in the telemetry parser would hand an attacker root inside that container, with every kernel feature root can reach.

Required: the service has no reason to be root. Recreate `telemetry` from `alpine:3.20` so it runs as user and group 1000:1000, and keep it running. I will check with `id`.

Remediation window: until the supply ship leaves Friday.
objectives: Remove the root-running container `telemetry`
Run a new container named `telemetry` from `alpine:3.20` with `sleep infinity`, in the background
It must run as user 1000 and group 1000
missions.startingState: A container `telemetry` (alpine:3.20, sleep infinity) is running as root.
hints: A container's user is chosen when it is created; you cannot turn a running root container into an unprivileged one. You have to replace it, and `docker run` has an option that sets the user and group the main process runs as.
The flag is `--user` (short form `-u`) and takes `UID:GID`. Remove the old container with `docker rm -f` first, because the name `telemetry` is taken.

```bash
docker rm -f telemetry
docker run -d --name telemetry --user 1000:1000 alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
docker exec telemetry id
```

commands: docker run -d --name telemetry alpine:3.20 sleep infinity

validation.description: The container is configured to run as `1000:1000`

solution: docker run -d --name telemetry --user 1000:1000 alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
missions.debrief: Running as a non-root user means an exploited process starts with far fewer powers, and `--user UID:GID` achieves that without rebuilding the image. Pro tip: use a numeric UID:GID rather than a name, because names only resolve if the image has a matching /etc/passwd entry.

missions.title: Carved in Stone
missions.story:
[RADIO -- INGRID TO ENGINEER, 06:40]

Engineer, Halvorsen. Wren just showed me that anything that gets a shell inside `ledger` can rewrite the ledger program itself. Tomasz's ice-core sample counts run through that service; if the code can be tampered with, nobody can trust the numbers.

Rebuild the container so its root filesystem is read-only. The service still needs somewhere to write its running log, so give it a RAM-backed `/tmp` and nothing more. Same port as before, 8140. Over.
objectives: Replace container `ledger` with a new one from `python:3.12-alpine`, publishing host port 8140 to container port 8000
Mount `/workspace/app` read-only at `/app` and run `python /app/ledger.py`
Make the root filesystem read-only, with a `tmpfs` at `/tmp`
http://localhost:8140 must still answer
missions.startingState: Container `ledger` runs the service with a writable root filesystem; the code is in `/workspace/app/ledger.py`.
hints: Docker can start a container with its whole root filesystem mounted read-only, so nothing can be changed or installed. Programs that need scratch space then require a separate writable location, and RAM-backed temporary mounts are the usual answer.

Use `--read-only` for the filesystem and `--tmpfs /tmp` for the one writable path. A container cannot be edited in place, so remove `ledger` first and recreate it with the same port and bind mount (`-v /workspace/app:/app:ro`).

```bash
docker rm -f ledger
docker run -d --name ledger --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
  -p 8140:8000 -v /workspace/app:/app:ro \
  python:3.12-alpine python /app/ledger.py
curl localhost:8140
```

files.content:
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

LOG = "/tmp/ledger.log"


class Ledger(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        with open(LOG, "a") as f:
            f.write("sample logged\n")
        with open(LOG) as f:
            entries = len(f.readlines())
        self.send_response(200)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(f"LEDGER OK entries={entries}\n".encode())


HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), Ledger).serve_forever()

validation.description: The root filesystem of `ledger` is read-only
Writing to the root filesystem (`/etc`) fails
http://localhost:8140 still answers with the ledger entry count

missions.debrief: With the root filesystem locked, an intruder cannot plant or alter a single binary, and `--tmpfs` still gives the service the scratch space it needs. Pro tip: when a program dies with 'Read-only file system', the error names the exact path that needs its own tmpfs or volume.

missions.title: Fewer Keys on the Ring
missions.story:
NORA: GATEKEEPER CAPABILITY COUNT 14
NORA: GATEKEEPER REQUIRED CAPABILITIES 1
NORA: AUDITOR WREN FLAGGED EXCESS PRIVILEGE

The `gatekeeper` container serves the crew login page on port 8150 and runs with Docker's default bundle of 14 Linux capabilities. Its only privileged act is binding to port 80 inside the container.

Wren's note, pinned beside the alert: "Least privilege is not a suggestion. Take every key off the ring, then hand back the one it needs." Recreate `gatekeeper` that way.
objectives: Replace container `gatekeeper` with one from `python:3.12-alpine`, publishing host port 8150 to container port 80
Run `python -m http.server 80 --directory /gate` with `/workspace/gate` mounted read-only at `/gate`
Drop ALL capabilities and add back only `NET_BIND_SERVICE`
The login page at http://localhost:8150 must still load
missions.startingState: Container `gatekeeper` is running with the default capability set; the login page lives in `/workspace/gate/`.
hints: Linux splits root's powers into separate capabilities, and Docker gives each container a default set of 14. You can remove capabilities when creating a container, and add specific ones back. Binding a port below 1024 is one such capability.

`--cap-drop ALL` removes the whole default set, and `--cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` returns the single one the web server needs. The order of the flags does not matter, but the container has to be recreated.

```bash
docker rm -f gatekeeper
docker run -d --name gatekeeper \
  --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  -p 8150:80 -v /workspace/gate:/gate:ro \
  python:3.12-alpine python -m http.server 80 --directory /gate
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.CapAdd}}' gatekeeper
```

files.content:
KESTREL POINT CREW LOGIN

Badge required.

commands: docker run -d --name gatekeeper -p 8150:80 -v /workspace/gate:/gate:ro python:3.12-alpine python -m http.server 80 --directory /gate

validation.description: All default capabilities are dropped (`CapDrop` contains ALL)
The main process holds only the bind-service capability
The crew login page still loads on port 8150

solution: docker run -d --name gatekeeper --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE -p 8150:80 -v /workspace/gate:/gate:ro python:3.12-alpine python -m http.server 80 --directory /gate
missions.debrief: Capabilities slice root into small privileges, and dropping ALL then adding back one by name is the strictest form of least privilege Docker offers. Pro tip: if a dropped container fails, its error message names what is missing, so add capabilities back one at a time rather than reaching for `--privileged`.

missions.title: Rationing
missions.story:
Sticky note on monitor 3, Amara's handwriting:

"cruncher went into a loop at 3am, spawned a few hundred processes and took the whole box with it. sorry!!

can you box it in? 256 MB of RAM, half a CPU, 64 processes max.
DO NOT restart it -- the glacier job is 80% done and I wrote the checkpoint file by hand. -- A."

Beneath it, in red pen, Wren has underlined "whole box" twice.
objectives: Limit the running container `cruncher` to 256 MB of memory
Limit it to 0.5 CPUs
Limit it to at most 64 processes
Do not recreate it: `/tmp/checkpoint` inside the container must survive
missions.startingState: Container `cruncher` (alpine:3.20) runs with no limits at all, and holds a checkpoint in `/tmp/checkpoint`.
hints: Resource limits are not only for new containers; Docker can change them on a running one. Restarting or recreating `cruncher` would lose the checkpoint that only exists inside it, so look for a command that edits a live container.
`docker update` accepts `--memory`, `--cpus` and `--pids-limit`. When you set a memory limit on a container that had none, set `--memory-swap` to the same value so swap does not exceed it.

```bash
docker update --memory 256m --memory-swap 256m --cpus 0.5 --pids-limit 64 cruncher
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}} {{.HostConfig.PidsLimit}}' cruncher
```

commands: docker run -d --name cruncher alpine:3.20 sleep infinity

validation.description: The original container (with its checkpoint) was not recreated

missions.debrief: Memory, CPU and process limits keep one runaway container from starving everything else on the host, and `docker update` applies them live without touching the container's state. Pro tip: `--pids-limit` is the cheap defence against fork bombs, and `docker stats` shows whether a limit is actually being hit.

missions.title: Secrets Belong in Files
missions.story:
**From:** Wren Achebe
**Subject:** F-05 -- credential visible to anyone who can run `docker inspect`

Engineer,

I ran `docker inspect uplink` and `docker history kestrel/uplink:1.0`. The satellite uplink's API key appears in plain text in both: it was baked into the image as an `ENV` line. Anyone who pulls this image owns the key.

Rebuild `kestrel/uplink:1.0` without it, and give the container the key as a read-only file at `/run/secrets/api_key`, taken from `/workspace/secrets/api_key.txt`. The program already knows how to read that file.

Rotating the key is Ingrid's job. Yours is making sure it is not in the image.

W.
objectives: Rebuild image `kestrel/uplink:1.0` from `/workspace` without the `API_KEY` environment variable in the image or its history
Replace container `uplink` with one from the new image, publishing host port 8160 to 8000
Bind-mount `/workspace/secrets/api_key.txt` read-only at `/run/secrets/api_key`
The container must not receive `API_KEY` as an environment variable
missions.startingState: `kestrel/uplink:1.0` was built with `ENV API_KEY=...` and container `uplink` runs on port 8160. The key file `secrets/api_key.txt` is ready.
hints: Anything in `ENV`, `ARG` or a `RUN` command becomes part of the image's metadata or history, and `docker inspect` shows a container's environment too. Secrets should arrive at runtime, as a file that is not part of the image.

Delete the `ENV API_KEY=...` line from the Dockerfile and rebuild the same tag. Then recreate the container with a bind mount of the key file onto `/run/secrets/api_key`, ending in `:ro`. Do not pass the key with `-e`.

```bash
sed -i '/^ENV API_KEY/d' Dockerfile
docker build -t kestrel/uplink:1.0 .
docker rm -f uplink
docker run -d --name uplink -p 8160:8000 \
  -v /workspace/secrets/api_key.txt:/run/secrets/api_key:ro \
  kestrel/uplink:1.0
```

files.content:
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /srv
ENV API_KEY=kp_live_9Q4xT2
COPY app.py .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
kp_live_9Q4xT2

validation.description: The image's environment no longer contains `API_KEY`
The image history no longer contains the key value
The container has no `API_KEY` environment variable
The key file is bind-mounted read-only at `/run/secrets/api_key`
The uplink authenticates using the mounted key

missions.debrief: Whatever you put in an image layer, `ENV` or `ARG` stays readable by anyone holding the image, so credentials belong in files mounted at runtime (Compose `secrets:` does the same thing). Pro tip: add secret paths to `.dockerignore` so they can never be copied in by accident, and rotate any key that was ever baked into an image.

missions.title: A Relay That Can't Escalate
missions.story:
**Kip:** quick question, what does USER do in a Dockerfile?

**Kip:** asking because Wren ran `docker run --rm --entrypoint id kestrel/safe-relay:1.0 -u` on my relay image and said a word I can't repeat in front of Ingrid. It printed 0.

**Kip:** she also wants the running container to have no-new-privileges, which I think means setuid tricks stop working? can you do the Dockerfile AND the container? Dockerfile and `relay.sh` are in /workspace. I'll watch and learn!
objectives: Edit the Dockerfile so image `kestrel/safe-relay:1.0` creates an unprivileged user and sets it with `USER`, then rebuild that tag
The image's default user must not be root
Replace container `relay` with one from the rebuilt image, started with `no-new-privileges`
The container's process must not run as uid 0
missions.startingState: `kestrel/safe-relay:1.0` was built from the Dockerfile in `/workspace` (no `USER` line); container `relay` runs from it as root.
hints: Without a `USER` instruction an image runs as root. Setting the user in the Dockerfile makes safe the default for everyone who runs the image, instead of relying on each person remembering a flag. The second requirement is a separate runtime setting, passed with `--security-opt`.

In the Dockerfile: create a user with Alpine's `addgroup -S` and `adduser -S`, then put `USER relay` before `CMD`. At runtime the option is `--security-opt no-new-privileges`. Rebuild the same tag and replace the old container.

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN addgroup -S relay && adduser -S -G relay relay
COPY relay.sh /usr/local/bin/relay.sh
USER relay
CMD ["sh", "/usr/local/bin/relay.sh"]
```

Then build and run:

```bash
docker build -t kestrel/safe-relay:1.0 .
docker rm -f relay
docker run -d --name relay --security-opt no-new-privileges kestrel/safe-relay:1.0
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY relay.sh /usr/local/bin/relay.sh
CMD ["sh", "/usr/local/bin/relay.sh"]

validation.description: The image sets a default user (`USER` in the Dockerfile)
Running the image's default configuration does not give uid 0
The process inside `relay` is not uid 0
The relay reports an unprivileged uid in its log

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN addgroup -S relay && adduser -S -G relay relay
COPY relay.sh /usr/local/bin/relay.sh
USER relay
CMD ["sh", "/usr/local/bin/relay.sh"]
EOF
missions.debrief: `USER` makes the safe choice the default for everyone who runs the image, and `no-new-privileges` stops setuid binaries from gaining more rights than the process started with -- two layers that work together. Pro tip: put `USER` after your `RUN` steps that need root (installing packages), so only the final runtime stage is unprivileged.

modules.title: The Satellite Link
modules.theme: Ship images over a tiny, unreliable link

missions.title: A Depot on the Ice
missions.story:
A yellow sticky note is taped to the server rack, in Ingrid Halvorsen's square handwriting:

"Satellite link: eleven minutes a day, billed by the megabyte. Every image we pull from the mainland gets paid for once, never twice. We need a depot here on the ice so that what we have already paid for stays on the station. It must survive a reboot, so keep its data on a named volume. - I.H."

Stand the depot up on port 5000.
objectives: Run a detached container named `depot` from `registry:2`
Publish host port `5000` to container port `5000`
Keep the registry's data in the named volume `depot-data`, mounted at `/var/lib/registry`
The registry API answers at `http://localhost:5000/v2/`
missions.startingState: A clean engine. The `registry:2` image is already on the machine.
hints: A registry is just another container: the official `registry:2` image speaks the same API as Docker Hub. You need a detached run, a published port, and somewhere durable for its data.

The registry stores everything under `/var/lib/registry`. Mount a named volume there with `-v NAME:/var/lib/registry`, publish the port with `-p 5000:5000`, and give the container the name `depot` with `--name`.

```bash
docker run -d --name depot \
  -p 5000:5000 \
  -v depot-data:/var/lib/registry \
  registry:2

curl http://localhost:5000/v2/
```

validation.description: Host port 5000 is published to container port 5000 of `depot`

missions.debrief: A registry stores image layers in one directory, so a volume under `/var/lib/registry` is all it takes to make the depot outlive its container. Pro tip: `curl http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog` lists everything the depot holds.

missions.title: First Shipment
missions.story:
NORA: `OUTBOUND QUEUE: 0 IMAGES. DEPOT: ONLINE. kestrel/beacon:1.0: LOCAL ONLY.`

The depot is up on port 5000, but the beacon image Amara built exists only on this one machine's disk. If the disk goes, the image goes with it, and Ingrid wants every instrument host to fetch its images from the depot instead.

Publish `kestrel/beacon:1.0` to the depot, under the registry's own address, so anyone on the station can pull it.
objectives: Tag `kestrel/beacon:1.0` as `localhost:5000/kestrel/beacon:1.0`
Push `localhost:5000/kestrel/beacon:1.0` to the depot
The depot's catalog lists the repository `kestrel/beacon` with the tag `1.0`
missions.startingState: The `depot` registry is running on port 5000 and the image `kestrel/beacon:1.0` is built locally. The depot is empty.
hints: Docker decides where to push by reading the registry host out of the image name. An image called `kestrel/beacon` means Docker Hub; to reach the depot, the same image needs a second name that starts with the registry's address.
Add the name with `docker tag SOURCE TARGET`, where TARGET is `HOST:PORT/repo/name:tag`. Then `docker push TARGET`. You can read back what the depot holds at `http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog`.

```bash
docker tag kestrel/beacon:1.0 localhost:5000/kestrel/beacon:1.0
docker push localhost:5000/kestrel/beacon:1.0

curl http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/beacon/tags/list
```

files.content:
FROM nginx:alpine
LABEL station=kestrel role=beacon
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
KESTREL POINT BEACON

validation.description: The depot has the tag `1.0` for `kestrel/beacon`
The manifest for `kestrel/beacon:1.0` can be fetched from the depot

missions.debrief: The registry host is part of an image's name, so pushing somewhere new always starts with `docker tag`. Pro tip: a tag is only a pointer, so tagging costs nothing and the push uploads each layer once.

missions.title: Round Trip
missions.story:
Station chat, 06:40.

**Tomasz:** The core-index image went up to the depot last night, and then Amara wiped the build machine. Before I stake the winter's index on that copy I need to know it is intact.

**Tomasz:** Pull it back from the depot. Then write its digest into `/workspace/digest.txt`, the sha256 exactly as the registry reports it, so I can compare it against my logbook. Precision, please.
objectives: Pull `localhost:5000/kestrel/core-index:1.0` from the depot
Write the image's `sha256:...` digest into `/workspace/digest.txt`, matching what the depot reports
missions.startingState: The depot holds `kestrel/core-index:1.0`, but no copy of it is on this machine any more.
hints: An image you have pushed lives on in the registry even when your local copy is gone. Pulling brings it back, and a digest is the content hash that proves it is the same bytes.

Pull with the full registry name. Afterwards `docker images --digests` shows the digest column, and `docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'` prints `name@sha256:...`. Only the part starting at `sha256:` belongs in the file.

```bash
docker pull localhost:5000/kestrel/core-index:1.0
docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' \
  localhost:5000/kestrel/core-index:1.0 | cut -d@ -f2 > digest.txt
cat digest.txt
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL station=kestrel role=core-index
CMD ["echo", "CORE INDEX 1.0 READY"]

validation.description: The image `localhost:5000/kestrel/core-index:1.0` is present locally again
The local image is the `core-index` image from the depot (label `role=core-index`)

params.command: d=$(tr -d ' \r\n' < /workspace/digest.txt); r=$(curl -sI -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json, application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/core-index/manifests/1.0 | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="docker-content-digest"{print $2}'); [ -n "$r" ] && echo "$d" | grep -qF "$r" && echo digest-matches

validation.description: The digest in `digest.txt` equals the manifest digest the depot reports for `kestrel/core-index:1.0`

missions.debrief: Tags can move, but a digest names exactly one set of bytes, so recording it is how you prove a transfer was faithful. Pro tip: pull or run `name@sha256:...` to pin an image to that exact digest, whatever the tag does later.

missions.title: Sneakernet
missions.story:
Radio, channel 9. Wind noise, then Captain Rafael Duarte of the *Petrel*:

"Kestrel Point, the relay is dead again and I sail at dawn. I can carry files. Put the ice-report image on a tar in the outbox and I will take it to the mainland. In return I have a tar from the mainland team with their patch kit. It is in your inbox already. Over."

No registry, no network: move the images the old way, as files.
objectives: Save the local image `kestrel/ice-report:3.2` to the tar file `/workspace/outbox/ice-report.tar`
Load `/workspace/inbox/mainland-patchkit.tar` so that the image `mainland/patchkit:7` exists
missions.startingState: `/workspace/outbox/` is empty and `/workspace/inbox/mainland-patchkit.tar` has arrived. The image `kestrel/ice-report:3.2` is built locally; `mainland/patchkit:7` is not on this machine.
hints: Images can travel as plain files. One command writes an image and its layers into a tar archive, and its counterpart reads such an archive back into the local engine.

Use `docker save -o FILE.tar IMAGE:TAG` to export (do not gzip it) and `docker load -i FILE.tar` to import. Remember the outbox is `/workspace/outbox/` and the delivered tar sits in `/workspace/inbox/`.

```bash
docker save -o outbox/ice-report.tar kestrel/ice-report:3.2
docker load -i inbox/mainland-patchkit.tar
docker images mainland/patchkit
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL station=kestrel role=ice-report
CMD ["echo", "ICE REPORT 3.2"]

FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL origin=mainland
CMD ["echo", "PATCHKIT 7"]

validation.description: The outbox tar is a Docker image archive containing `kestrel/ice-report:3.2`

missions.debrief: `docker save` and `docker load` turn images into ordinary files, which is how images cross an air gap on a ship, a USB stick or anything else. Pro tip: pass several image names to one `docker save` to bundle them, and they share layers inside the tar.

missions.title: Many Names, One Image
missions.story:
Kip's release checklist, copied from the whiteboard:

`[x] build kestrel/forecast:2.1.0`
`[ ] push 2.1.0`
`[ ] push 2.1, 2 and latest`
`[ ] tell Ingrid`

Amara spots the catch: the depot's `latest` still points at last week's 2.0.0, and every instrument host follows `latest`. Give the release all four names in the depot, 2.1.0, 2.1, 2 and latest, and make sure they are one and the same image.
objectives: Publish `kestrel/forecast:2.1.0` to the depot as `localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:2.1.0`
Also publish it as `2.1`, `2` and `latest` under `localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast`
All four tags resolve to the same manifest digest in the depot
missions.startingState: The depot already holds `kestrel/forecast` with the tags `2.0.0` and `latest` (both the old release). The new `kestrel/forecast:2.1.0` exists only locally.
hints: A release usually carries several names: a full version, shorter version prefixes, and a moving `latest`. They are all just tags, so one image can wear them all, and re-pushing a tag moves it.

Give the local image one extra name per tag with `docker tag SOURCE localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:TAG`, then push each. Compare tags by asking the registry for each manifest's `Docker-Content-Digest` header.

```bash
for t in 2.1.0 2.1 2 latest; do
  docker tag kestrel/forecast:2.1.0 localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:$t
  docker push localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:$t
done
curl http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/forecast/tags/list
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL station=kestrel service=forecast version=2.0.0
CMD ["echo", "forecast 2.0.0"]

FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL station=kestrel service=forecast version=2.1.0
CMD ["echo", "forecast 2.1.0"]

validation.description: The depot lists the tags `2.1.0`, `2.1`, `2` and `latest` for `kestrel/forecast`

params.command: out=$(for t in 2.1.0 2.1 2 latest; do curl -sI -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json, application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/forecast/manifests/$t | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="docker-content-digest"{print $2}'; done); [ "$(echo "$out" | grep -c sha256)" = 4 ] && [ "$(echo "$out" | sort -u | wc -l)" = 1 ] && echo all-same

validation.description: All four tags (`2.1.0`, `2.1`, `2`, `latest`) have the same manifest digest in the depot

params.command: [ "$(curl -sI -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json, application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/forecast/manifests/latest | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="docker-content-digest"{print $2}')" != "$(curl -sI -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json, application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/forecast/manifests/2.0.0 | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="docker-content-digest"{print $2}')" ] && echo moved

validation.description: `latest` no longer points at the old `2.0.0` release
The local image has the name `localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:latest`

modules.title: Polar Night
modules.theme: Advanced tooling, resilience and cleanup for the long dark

missions.title: Don't Download Twice
missions.story:
**From:** Amara Okafor
**Subject:** climate-fetch rebuilds are eating the satellite budget

Every time I touch one line of `requirements.txt`, pip downloads every package again. The Dockerfile even has `--no-cache-dir` in it, because someone once told me that keeps images small. Ten rebuilds a day over a metered link adds up fast.

Can you make the build keep pip's download cache between builds, without baking the cache into the image? Build the result as `kestrel/climate-fetch:1.0`.
objectives: Edit `/workspace/Dockerfile` so the pip install step uses a BuildKit cache mount on `/root/.cache/pip`
Remove `--no-cache-dir` from the install step
Build the image as `kestrel/climate-fetch:1.0`; it must still run and print `climate-fetch ready`
missions.startingState: `/workspace` holds a working Dockerfile, `requirements.txt` and `fetch.py` for the climate-fetch tool, but nothing has been built yet.
hints: The build engine (BuildKit) can mount a directory that persists between builds but never becomes part of an image layer. That is exactly what a package manager's download cache needs.
Attach it to the install step with `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=DIR ...`. pip's cache lives in `/root/.cache/pip`, and `--no-cache-dir` would tell pip to ignore it, so it has to go.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY fetch.py .
CMD ["python", "fetch.py"]
```
Then `docker build -t kestrel/climate-fetch:1.0 .`

files.content:
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY fetch.py .
CMD ["python", "fetch.py"]
python-dateutil==2.9.0.post0

import dateutil.parser
print('climate-fetch ready', dateutil.parser.parse('2026-06-21').year)

validation.description: The Dockerfile installs with `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip` and without `--no-cache-dir`

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY fetch.py .
CMD ["python", "fetch.py"]
EOF
missions.debrief: The second build skipped the download because the cache mount survived between builds, and it never became part of a layer, so the image stays lean. Pro tip: the same trick works for `apk` (`/var/cache/apk`), Go (`/root/.cache/go-build`) and `npm`.

missions.title: Whisper to the Builder
missions.story:
Excerpt from the mainland's image-scan report on `kestrel/uplink:0.9`:

`FINDING HIGH  layer 2  ARG MAINLAND_TOKEN=KP-4e9b... is readable with docker history`

The uplink build has to prove it can authenticate, so it really does need the mainland token while it builds. But the token must not survive in any layer, environment variable or history line. The token file is `/workspace/secrets/mainland.token`.

Rewrite the Dockerfile so BuildKit hands the token over as a secret, and build `kestrel/uplink:1.0`.
objectives: Rewrite `/workspace/Dockerfile` to read the token through `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mainland_token` and drop the `ARG`
Build `kestrel/uplink:1.0` passing `secrets/mainland.token` as the secret `mainland_token`
The build still wrote `token-ok` to `/opt/uplink-status`, but the token appears nowhere in the image or its history
missions.startingState: `/workspace/Dockerfile` is the leaky version that takes the token as `ARG MAINLAND_TOKEN`; `/workspace/secrets/mainland.token` holds the token. No image has been built.
hints: Build arguments and environment variables are recorded in image metadata forever. BuildKit has a different channel: a secret is mounted for a single `RUN` step as a temporary file and leaves no trace.

In the Dockerfile, add `--mount=type=secret,id=NAME` to the `RUN` that needs it; the value appears as the file `/run/secrets/NAME`. At build time supply it with `docker build --secret id=NAME,src=FILE`.

```dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mainland_token \
    grep -q '^KP-' /run/secrets/mainland_token \
    && echo token-ok > /opt/uplink-status
CMD ["cat", "/opt/uplink-status"]
```
```bash
docker build -t kestrel/uplink:1.0 \
  --secret id=mainland_token,src=secrets/mainland.token .
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
ARG MAINLAND_TOKEN
RUN echo "$MAINLAND_TOKEN" | grep -q '^KP-' && echo token-ok > /opt/uplink-status
CMD ["cat", "/opt/uplink-status"]
KP-4e9b27d1-polar-7781

validation.description: The Dockerfile uses `--mount=type=secret,id=mainland_token` and no longer declares `ARG MAINLAND_TOKEN`
The build consumed the token: `/opt/uplink-status` in the image contains `token-ok`
The token does not appear in `docker history --no-trunc kestrel/uplink:1.0`

params.command: if docker image inspect kestrel/uplink:1.0 | grep -q KP-4e9b27d1- || docker run --rm --entrypoint sh kestrel/uplink:1.0 -c 'grep -rsq KP-4e9b27d1- /etc /opt /root /home /tmp /var /usr /app'; then echo LEAK; else echo CLEAN; fi

validation.description: The token is not stored in the image metadata (env, labels) or anywhere in its filesystem

solution:
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mainland_token \
    grep -q '^KP-' /run/secrets/mainland_token \
    && echo token-ok > /opt/uplink-status
CMD ["cat", "/opt/uplink-status"]
EOF
missions.debrief: A `--build-arg` or `ENV` is written into the image for everyone who can pull it, while a secret mount exists only for the one `RUN` step that asks for it. Pro tip: `--secret id=x,env=VAR` reads the secret from an environment variable instead of a file.

missions.title: A Graceful Goodbye
missions.story:
NORA: `TIDE-LOGGER STOP TOOK 10.0 S. EXIT CODE 137. LAST FLUSH: NEVER. ORPHANED PROCESSES: 41.`

The tide logger keeps its readings in memory and only writes them out when it receives SIGINT. Docker's default stop sends SIGTERM, which the logger ignores, so after ten seconds the engine kills it and a night of readings is lost. It also leaves defunct child processes behind, because nothing reaps them.

Replace the running `tide-logger` container: give it a proper init process, SIGINT as its stop signal, and a 20-second grace period.
objectives: Remove the old `tide-logger` container and run a new detached `tide-logger` from `kestrel/tide-logger:1.0`
Run it with Docker's built-in init process (`--init`)
Stop signal `SIGINT`, grace period of `20` seconds before the kill
missions.startingState: The image `kestrel/tide-logger:1.0` is built and a naive container `tide-logger` is running from it with default settings.
hints: Two separate problems: the process at PID 1 does not forward or reap anything, and `docker stop` sends a signal the application does not handle. Both are fixed with options on the container, no code changes.

`--init` puts a tiny init program at PID 1. `--stop-signal SIGINT` changes the signal `docker stop` sends, and `--stop-timeout SECONDS` changes how long it waits before SIGKILL. These are `docker run` flags, so the old container has to be replaced.

```bash
docker rm -f tide-logger
docker run -d --name tide-logger \
  --init \
  --stop-signal SIGINT \
  --stop-timeout 20 \
  kestrel/tide-logger:1.0

docker stop tide-logger && docker logs tide-logger | tail -2
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
COPY logger.sh /logger.sh
RUN chmod +x /logger.sh
CMD ["/logger.sh"]

#!/bin/sh
buf=0
flush() { echo "FLUSHED $buf readings"; exit 0; }
trap flush INT
echo "tide-logger started"
while true; do
  buf=$((buf + 1))
  ( sleep 1 & )
  sleep 1
done

validation.description: `tide-logger` has a stop timeout of 20 seconds
PID 1 inside `tide-logger` is the init process, not the logger script

missions.debrief: `docker stop` is a polite request (the stop signal) followed by a deadline (the timeout); if your program answers to a different signal, change the request rather than the program. Pro tip: put `STOPSIGNAL SIGINT` in the Dockerfile to make the right signal the image's default.

missions.title: The Other Station
missions.story:
Ingrid, on the handheld radio, voice thin against the wind:

"Engineer, the hut at Skua Ridge keeps a second Docker engine as our fallback. When we need it, it will be midnight and somebody will be typing endpoints from memory. I don't want that. Give the hut a name the CLI understands, and prove the name works by starting a probe container there. The cable isn't laid yet, so for now point it at the endpoint in `/workspace/hut-endpoint.txt`. Over."
objectives: Create a context named `backup-station` for the endpoint in `/workspace/hut-endpoint.txt`, with the description `Backup hut engine`
Make `backup-station` the active context with `docker context use`
Through that context, run a detached `hut-probe` container from `alpine:3.20` that sleeps (`sleep infinity`)
missions.startingState: Only the `default` context exists. The file `/workspace/hut-endpoint.txt` holds the endpoint to use.
hints: The Docker CLI can talk to several engines. A context bundles an endpoint with a name, so switching engines is one short command instead of environment variables or long flags.
Create it with `docker context create NAME --docker host=ENDPOINT --description TEXT`, then switch to it with `docker context use NAME`. `docker context ls` marks the active one with an asterisk.

```bash
docker context create backup-station \
  --docker host=$(cat hut-endpoint.txt) \
  --description "Backup hut engine"
docker context use backup-station
docker context show
docker run -d --name hut-probe alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
```

files.content: unix:///var/run/docker.sock

validation.description: A context `backup-station` exists and points at `unix:///var/run/docker.sock`
The context `backup-station` has the description `Backup hut engine`
`backup-station` is the active context (`docker context use backup-station`)

solution: docker context create backup-station --docker host=unix:///var/run/docker.sock --description 'Backup hut engine'
docker run -d --name hut-probe alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
missions.debrief: Switching engines is now one word instead of a remembered socket path: the context bundles endpoint and description under a name. Pro tip: `docker --context NAME ps` runs a single command elsewhere without changing the active context.

missions.title: A Swarm in the Dark
missions.story:
The aurora forecast printout on the corkboard has a circled line in Tomasz's tidy handwriting:

`KP index 8 tonight. Expect every screen on the station, plus the mainland, on the aurora page.`

Beneath it Ingrid has added, in pen: "One container will fall over. Three copies, spread by the engine, one front door for all of them. Use swarm."

Turn this engine into a swarm and publish the `aurora-feed` service on port 8090, with three replicas of `nginx:alpine`.
objectives: Initialise Docker Swarm on this engine
Create the service `aurora-feed` from `nginx:alpine` with `3` replicas
Publish host port `8090` to container port `80` through the service
All three replicas are running and `http://localhost:8090` answers
missions.startingState: A plain engine, not part of any swarm. `nginx:alpine` is already on the machine.
hints: Swarm mode turns one engine into a cluster manager that schedules services rather than single containers. You first switch the mode on, and then describe the service you want kept alive.

`docker swarm init` enables it (add `--advertise-addr 127.0.0.1` if Docker complains about several addresses). Then `docker service create --name NAME --replicas N -p HOST:CONTAINER IMAGE`. `--detach=false` makes the command wait for convergence.

```bash
docker swarm init
docker service create --detach=false \
  --name aurora-feed \
  --replicas 3 \
  -p 8090:80 \
  nginx:alpine
docker service ls
```

validation.description: Swarm mode is active on this engine
Service `aurora-feed` has 3 replicas of `nginx:alpine`, all running

solution: docker swarm init --advertise-addr 127.0.0.1 || docker swarm init
missions.debrief: A service is a desired state, so swarm keeps replacing replicas until reality matches the number you declared. Pro tip: the published port works on every swarm node via the routing mesh, whichever node actually runs a replica.

missions.title: Change the Watch
missions.story:
Station chat, after the aurora page went white.

**Kip:** I pushed the new feed image to all three replicas at once and the whole page was down for forty seconds. Sorry!

**Ingrid:** Nobody does it that way again. One replica at a time, a short pause between each, and if the new version fails to come up, the old one goes back on its own. Engineer, roll `aurora-feed` onto `nginx:alpine` the proper way, and make those rules part of the service so they apply next time too.
objectives: Update the running service `aurora-feed` to the image `nginx:alpine`
Set the update parallelism to `1` and the update delay to `5s`
Set the update failure action to `rollback`
The service still has 3 running replicas and the update has completed
missions.startingState: A swarm is running with the service `aurora-feed` (3 replicas of `nginx:1.27-alpine`, port 8091). It has never been updated.
hints: A swarm service is replaced task by task. How fast, how many at once, and what happens on failure are properties of the service's update configuration, and they apply to this update and every later one.

Use `docker service update` on the existing service. Relevant flags: `--image`, `--update-parallelism N`, `--update-delay DURATION`, `--update-failure-action rollback`. `--detach=false` waits until the rollout finishes.

```bash
docker service update --detach=false \
  --image nginx:alpine \
  --update-parallelism 1 \
  --update-delay 5s \
  --update-failure-action rollback \
  aurora-feed

docker service inspect aurora-feed --pretty
```

commands: docker swarm init --advertise-addr 127.0.0.1 || docker swarm init

validation.description: The update failure action of `aurora-feed` is `rollback`

params.command: for i in $(seq 14); do s=$(docker service inspect aurora-feed --format '{{.UpdateStatus.State}}'); [ "$s" = completed ] && break; sleep 1; done; echo $s

validation.description: The rolling update of `aurora-feed` has completed

solution: docker service update --detach=false --image nginx:alpine --update-parallelism 1 --update-delay 5s --update-failure-action rollback aurora-feed
missions.debrief: Swarm swapped the tasks one at a time, with a pause between them, so the feed never went fully dark, and a failed task would have triggered a rollback. Pro tip: `docker service rollback aurora-feed` undoes the last update by hand.

missions.title: Clearing the Snowdrifts
missions.story:
Ingrid's pre-winter checklist, last page:

`[ ] free disk space: the engine is at 94%`
`[ ] keep everything labelled keep=true (Tomasz's cores)`
`[ ] keep whatever is running or in use`

Tomasz has labelled the three things he cannot lose: a stopped container, a volume and an image, all `keep=true`. Everything else that nobody is using must go: stopped containers, unused volumes and dangling images. A bare `prune` would take his data with it, so use label filters.
objectives: Remove every stopped container except `keeper-log` (label `keep=true`)
Remove every unused volume except `ledger-vol` (label `keep=true`); `gauge-data` is in use and must stay
Remove every dangling image except the one labelled `keep=true`
Leave the running container `snow-gauge` and the tagged images `kestrel/drift:latest` and `kestrel/ledger-snap:latest` untouched
missions.startingState: Three throwaway stopped containers, two unused volumes and a few dangling images are mixed in with the things that must survive. A container `snow-gauge` is running and uses the volume `gauge-data`.
hints: Docker has a `prune` command for each kind of object. Pruning removes only what is unused, and most prune commands accept filters, so you can exclude anything carrying a particular label.

Try `docker container prune`, `docker volume prune` and `docker image prune`, each with `-f` and `--filter "label!=keep=true"`. Since Docker 23, `volume prune` skips named volumes unless you add `--all` (`-a`). Check with `docker ps -a`, `docker volume ls` and `docker images -f dangling=true`.

```bash
docker container prune -f --filter "label!=keep=true"
docker volume prune -af --filter "label!=keep=true"
docker image prune -f --filter "label!=keep=true"

docker ps -a
docker volume ls
docker images -f dangling=true
```

commands: docker run -d --name snow-gauge -v gauge-data:/data alpine:3.20 sleep infinity
for i in 1 2 3; do docker run --name drift-$i alpine:3.20 true; done
docker run --name keeper-log --label keep=true alpine:3.20 true
for v in 1 2; do printf "FROM alpine:3.20\nRUN echo snow-$v > /marker\n" | docker build -q -f - . ; done
printf 'FROM alpine:3.20\nRUN echo drift-tag > /marker\n' | docker build -q -t kestrel/drift:latest -f - .

printf 'FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL keep=true
RUN echo ledger-old > /marker
' | docker build -q -f - .

printf 'FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL keep=true
RUN echo ledger-tag > /marker
' | docker build -q -t kestrel/ledger-snap:latest -f - .

validation.description: Only `keeper-log` remains among the stopped containers

params.command: echo "$(docker images -f dangling=true -q | wc -l | tr -d ' ')/$(docker images -f dangling=true -f label=keep=true -q | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"

validation.description: Exactly one dangling image remains, and it is the one labelled `keep=true`

missions.debrief: Each `prune` removes only what is unused, and `--filter label!=...` lets you fence off whatever you labelled to protect. Pro tip: `--filter until=720h` limits a prune to objects older than 30 days, which makes a safe scheduled job.
